speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In my speech, I acknowledged that much effort has been made by the Government throughout the years in the preservation and strengthening of family ties, since it is the fabric of our nation.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This year, we see our national plan, "A Singapore Made for Families 2025" (MFF 2025), which builds on the momentum of the Year of Celebrating SG Families in 2022.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I quote extracts from Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat's foreword on this national plan: "Family has always been at the heart of our social compact.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We achieved this as a society, as a whole, is deeply committed to supporting families.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But there are greater challenges that families face, such as greater caregiving needs as our population ages rapidly, greater demands at our workplaces, higher cost of living pressures and more.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, we must explore new ways to support our families.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is a key national priority under the Forward Singapore exercise to refresh our social compact.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: MFF 2025 is our plan for creating a Singapore that values and supports family well-being." Indeed, over the past five years since the launch of MFF 2025, as a young parent myself, I am delighted to see and have benefited from many bolder changes in the policies that were rolled out by the Government in this aspect.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many innovative ideas and suggestions, calling for more versatile changes, such as the flexible Shared Parental Leave, were also adopted along the way.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To this end, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong's 2025 Chinese New Year message reinforces the Government's commitment in supporting families, and I quote: "Families are the bedrock of our society.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They nurture our values, provide emotional support and inspire us to dream big.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In today's fast-paced and competitive world, balancing work and family life has become harder.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yet, families remain at the heart of what matters most to us.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am encouraged that many Singaporeans continue to prioritise marriage, parenthood and family.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The Government is committed to supporting families at every stage of life.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For young couples, we are ramping up the supply of Build-To-Order (BTO) flats and making public housing more affordable.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We are enhancing leave arrangements, including through a new Shared Parental Leave scheme.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is a historic low, notwithstanding the Government's continuous efforts in supporting families.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These are worrying trends which present, in Minister Indranee Rajah's words, "serious implications" for our country's future.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This Motion, led by my Parliamentary colleague, Mr Zhulkarnain and I, is a continuous effort by us to review and update policies, and a continuation of our commitment to Singaporeans as well as rallying a call by this House to the whole of society to build a "Singapore Made for Families".

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I had acknowledged in my speech on the Child Development Co-Savings (Amendment) Bill (CDCA Bill) in November last year that prospective parents would have varying concerns and reasons militating against or for delaying starting a family.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In the People's Action Party (PAP) Women's Wing, we have been investigating the reasons underlying these phenomena, not least by engaging our constituents individually and through various platforms and forums.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Our research group had conducted several rounds of surveys, with the most recent involving over 1,000 married individuals, where the policy group collaborated with Friendzone to organise a series of heart-to-heart focused group discussions with youths aged between 20 and 40 years on topics, such as dating, relationship, marriage and parenthood.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I welcome my Parliamentary colleagues who will come forward to speak on this Motion, to join me in sharing the issues faced and perceived by Singaporeans that may impede or delay marriage and parenthood and share some possible solutions that we have distilled through our respective engagements.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One of the common strands of feedback I have received from Singaporeans who aspire towards marriage and eventual parenthood, is the challenge they face in finding the right partner.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This could be due to a lack of socialising opportunities or social spaces, being occupied with work or caretaking obligations at home, amongst other reasons.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In this regard, some Singaporeans have shared their hope for the return of the Singapore Social Development Network (SDN) or some other form of Government-led and encouraged social interaction platform with the objective of leading to marriage.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Granted, the present-day social and dating landscape is markedly different from when the Social Development Unit (SDU) was set up in 1984, before I was born, and to which the SDN traces its roots, the advent of technology and shifting socialising and dating norms have been growing acceptance or even popularity of online dating.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The same survey also found a significant increase in acceptance of meeting one's prospective partner on dating sites or apps.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Could we, therefore, synthesise the purport of SDN with technology and Singaporeans' current dating mindsets, to produce a solution?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To this end, we could perhaps draw some inspiration from China's state-sponsored matchmaking efforts.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In the city of Guixi in China's Jiangxi province, an app known as "Palm Guixi" was launched to function as a matchmaking platform.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The app matches users based on their background information and also assists to organise blind dates.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In fact, following one of the PAP Women's Wing’s collaborations with Friendzone focus group discussions that I had attended, one of the attendees, Jasper, shared with me that he has had a similar idea for an app, where singles provide answers to a set of questions which will be fed into a matching algorithm that matches singles based on their personal priorities amongst other attributes, such as desired age group.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Achieving a match would not, however, be the end-all and be-all, as the app could, and correctly should, facilitate follow-throughs, such as by recommending or helping to book dates at restaurants or other activities, based on the matched couple's shared interests.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Such a Government-led app would be distinguished from other dating apps, not least because it would likely provide prospective participants with assurance on trustworthiness and reliability, a point shared by another attendee, Christopher, who, also after the session, wrote to me to share that the SDU, or its current incarnation, can further evolve and serve as a platform that works with public and private agencies, including professional matchmaking or dating agencies, to organise events and create safe social spaces for young adults to bond over common interests.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I concur with Christopher, creating opportunities to encourage the young to learn and play together, perhaps through sports, such as pickleball, would be a good follow-through on the app's achievements.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Once a couple has been formed, we hope that they would share a blissful and everlasting relationship, and who will, together, go on to attain the milestones of marriage and starting a family.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I quote an extract from Prime Minister Lawrence Wong's speech at the launch of the National Family Festival on 25 May 2024: "I firmly believe that the true measure of success in life is not based on one's status or material possessions.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Instead, the richest treasures are the moments we share with our family members and loved ones – these relationships are our legacies and the truest reflections of our lives' worth.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, let us all pledge to cherish and nurture our family bonds.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Let us work together to build a "Singapore Made for Families", where we can create many happy memories with our families and where everyone can enjoy an enriching family life here in this Garden City we call home." I could not have said it better myself.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The concept of a "home" embodies so much more than acquiring a "house".

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Though admittedly, many Singaporeans feel that one of the first few steps, if not the first, is to acquire and get a place of their own.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For first-time home buyers, they receive at least two ballot chances as opposed to the one ballot chance for second-time families.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: HDB has also allocated the majority of 3-room and larger HDB flats for them.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: An additional ballot is given to these families in addition to the two ballot chances given to first-timer families.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There are also other schemes designed to increase the chances of getting a house for eligible families, such as the Family and Parenthood Priority Scheme, Married Child Priority Scheme and Third Child Priority Scheme.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Especially, if looked at against the backdrop of Singapore's housing demand and supply, the Government's housing policy is laudable.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, the mindset of the Government and this House, must always be the relentless pursuit of improvements.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At my Meet-the-People Sessions (MPS) in the PAP Woodgrove branch, I frequently receive requests for assistance from residents who aspire to start their families but are understandably anxious due to the waiting times and costs involved in getting a house, which to their minds, is the essential first step in building a home.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This could go a great length to ease part of the financial burdens and pressure on new parents, whose primary focus should rightly be on their newborn.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Furthermore and/or alternatively, the same arrangement should also be considered to be extended to large young families, until the youngest child enters primary school education.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We must not only actually do better in terms of policy-making, but also do our best to keep Singaporeans informed, in order to provide assurance and certainty, which would be essential to Singaporeans' family planning.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This brings me to my next topic – welcoming a new child to the family.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Child-bearing and child-raising are, in my view, the noblest of pursuits in life.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Children are the element that completes a family unit.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The critical message that this House and the Government ought to convey to every Singaporean, is that none of you – whether as a single parent or as a married couple – would ever feel alone in this rewarding and fulfilling journey.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The typical Singaporean who is aspiring to become a parent would invariably ask him or herself, "How am I going to cope with a newborn on top of my work?", "Would I have to drastically change my lifestyle to accommodate my baby?", "Will my quality of life drop if I have kids?", "what is the quality of life that I would be able to provide my child with?", amongst other questions.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These were also the questions that I pondered on when I was deciding whether to have more kids.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To varying degrees in a myriad of ways, the lives of both moms and dads are changed forever whenever a child joins the family.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: My Parliamentary colleague Mr Zhulkarnain will be sharing more in the aspect for the challenges that many fathers encounter during this journey later in his speech.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This House recognises the challenges of starting and expanding a family, and so does the Government, as evidenced by its constant improvements to its policies.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For example, I shared earlier, the Baby Bonus Scheme comprising the Baby Bonus Cash Gift and the Child Development Account (CDA) benefits is provided as soon as the child is born.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The Baby Bonus Scheme was most recently enhanced in 2023.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There is also the MediSave Grant for Newborns, which sees to it that a CPF MediSave account is opened for each newborn and the grant is credited automatically.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This grant provides support for each child's healthcare expenses, including MediShield premiums, recommended childhood vaccinations, hospitalisations and approved outpatient treatments.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Adding to the comprehensive coverage is the MediShield Life Coverage for Newborns and Fully-Subsidised Nationally-Recommended Childhood Vaccinations and Developmental Screenings.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As our children grow, we also get to utilise education subsidies totaling up to $180,000.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Most recently, through the CDCA Bill passed by this House in November last year, enhancements were made to the Parental Leave.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There is also the new Shared Parental Leave, which will entitle working parents who are eligible for Government-Paid Maternity Leave, Paternity Leave and Adoption Leave, to Shared Parental Leave.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There is also a built-in mechanism to allow for flexibility based on each family’s needs and taking into account the parents' employers' operational requirements.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But soon-to-be, as well as new parents would still be saddled with so much, and be under constant and immense pressure.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It would not be reasonable to expect them to be constantly aware and keep track of this policy developments made to assist them on their own.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To this end, I reiterate a suggestion I had made during the debate on Budget Statement in 2021, to call for the introduction of a "Mommy's Milestone Booklet".

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This booklet would be akin to a baby's health booklet but instead, would help to track the expecting mother's physical and emotional development.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It would also contain helpful information regarding necessary preparations for each stage of pregnancy, parenting best practices and a list of support systems available to all parents at least for the first years of their journey into parenthood, along with a checklist of vaccinations required for expecting mothers, recommended estimated dates to sign up for prenatal classes, a checklist of items to prepare for the arrival of the baby, tips on how to spot signs of labour and how to spot signs of post-natal depression.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This booklet could be similar to the Families for Life Parenting, a one-stop portal for parenting resources, but personalised to each family's needs and with relevant information conveyed to the parents-to-be by professionals at each milestone basis.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Another suggestion which has been frequently brought up by young parents, particularly those who are staying in BTO flats, concerns the challenges they face in securing a preschool spot for their toddlers.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This has been a problem which my Woodgrove residents in the Champions Court and Champions Green area have been encountering.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To cushion the operating costs of the Anchor Operators during this period, HDB can consider offering rent-free or higher subsidised rent rate until the enrolment rate achieves a certain desired number.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: (In Mandarin):   At the recent dialogues organised by PAP's Women's Wing, several participants provided feedback and suggestions to me.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As this year is Singapore's 60th birthday, they asked if the Government could consider providing more cash incentives from this year onwards, to encourage and assist Singaporeans in achieving important family-building milestones.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One participant suggested that we could call this a Kickstart Fund.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As we all know, even though the Government already provides many grants, subsidies and assistance for marriage, home ownership and parenthood, there are still many expenses that require cash payment.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For many young couples, it might be seen as a long-term burden, a process that is mixed with moments of joy, and mental and financial stress.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Overall, when building a family-friendly Singapore, I hope the Government can understand why Singaporeans are afraid of having children.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We should continue to listen to the people's concerns and as time and lifestyle evolves, be bold in introducing novel, yet practical measures to support Singaporeans in building their beautiful families. : Mr Speaker, in conclusion, I am heartened by the Government's commitment and continuing efforts to cultivate an environment that supports Singaporeans in starting and raising a family.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I look forward to my Parliamentary colleagues' speeches as well as a fruitful debate on this Motion.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: When Ms Hany Soh approached me to sponsor this Motion, I fully and readily supported it.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I have four children of my own, ranging from toddlers to teenagers.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, this means, for the past 16 years, I have experienced various stages of their childhood and hence, these eye bags as well.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I was blessed with my extended family support in this parenting journey and it helped a lot.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, I strongly believe in strengthening support for our family units in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I raised this in my maiden Parliamentary speech when I likened our nation building to Lego bricks: creating a myriad of structures from different shapes, sizes and colours and that our nation is strong only when each of our basic building block, the family unit, is strong.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In my speech, I am focusing on support for fathers as partners in raising a family.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Research consistently highlights the critical role fathers play in child development.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In 2020, the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) reported that children with actively involved fathers showed better emotional resilience and social skills.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Additionally, a 2019 study by the National University of Singapore (NUS) found that fathers who spent more time with their children contributed to higher levels of family satisfaction and lower rates of marital conflict.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, traditional gender roles and workplace cultures often limit fathers' ability to participate fully in child-raising.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Globally, fathers face challenges, such as stigma around taking paternity leave, lack of flexible work arrangements (FWAs) and societal expectations that prioritise mothers as primary caregivers.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We need to change that mindset of child caregiving amongst men, amongst society to encourage more to have children and raise a family.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To do so, we need to implement changes both at work and at home.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Globally, as well, paternity leave uptake is similarly low, with only about 34% of countries offering it and even fewer enforcing it as mandatory.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To address these, employers can offer FWAs, which has been shown to boost employee retention and satisfaction by 30%.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Incentives, like tax breaks or increased foreign manpower quotas, could encourage businesses to adopt family-friendly policies.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These measures could also apply to childcare leave, which currently offers six days for children under seven years, and two days extended childcare leave for those aged seven to 12.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For instance, those with two or more children, can be eligible for 10 days of childcare leave.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This covers key milestones in our children's lives, like entrance to kindergarten, Primary 1 registration and the Primary School Leaving Examination (PSLE), not to mention, other important events in their lives, like medical appointments and birthdays.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These changes, aligned with the 2023 PAP's Women's Wing and Young PAP joint paper, which advocates for expanded leave provisions and employer support for caregiving roles.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Additionally, stronger enforcement of anti-discrimination laws is needed to protect fathers taking leave or requesting FWAs as countries with robust protections see a 20% increase in fathers' involvement.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Beyond the workplace, Mr Speaker, we also need to change the perspectives of men in caregiving within our society.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In many societies, including Singapore, caregiving is still seen as primarily a mother's role.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: An Institute of Policy Studies (IPS) 2020 study found that 60% of fathers felt societal pressure to prioritise work over family.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A 2021 global survey revealed that 63% of men in Asia Pacific countries felt that society views them as less masculine if they take on caregiving roles.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Changing societal and workplace mindsets is crucial to encourage greater father involvement.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This includes redefining masculinity, in promoting the idea that caregiving is a strength, not a weakness, and that involved fatherhood is a key aspect of our modern world.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We also need to normalise shared parenting by encouraging both parents to take equal responsibility for child-raising.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this regard, I welcome the Government's move towards implementing six weeks of shared parenting.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This signifies a move towards recognising that the role of caregiving for children does not fall on the shoulders of mothers alone, but it is a shared responsibility of both parents together.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How the couple shares that load or childcare leave, is left to them.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, we can incentivise equitable sharing of such parenting leave by drawing from the lessons learnt in other jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We can encourage shared leave by introducing financial incentives, such as tax breaks or childcare subsidies, for families where both parents take equal childcare leave.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In Sweden, its "Daddy Month" policy, which reserves a portion of parental leave exclusively for fathers, has been highly effective.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: That being said, government policies alone will not change mindsets on child caregiving.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For parents, there are many other things that we ourselves can do to make the most of our time we spend with our children.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Families can create structured plans to divide caregiving responsibilities equitably.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, fathers can take on specific roles, such as bedtime routines, read your story books before bedtime, school drop-offs in the morning, to build consistent involvement daily with their children.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Couples should practise open communication and align their expectations about caregiving roles.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: At the community level, we can launch campaigns to normalise father involvement and challenge stereotypes through the involvement of "Dads for Life" or the vernacular "Bapa Sepanjang Hayat” movement to reach out to more workplaces and increase community engagement.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Fathers who participated in community programmes such as these, reported higher levels of confidence and involvement.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We can establish "Dad Hubs" in neighbourhoods to provide parenting resources and support.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this regard, at Keat Hong, we have been organising, for many years, annual talks and workshops for men on Breaking the Patriarchal Mindset in families, supported by MSF and organised by Casa Raudha Women Home.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is to normalise caregiving and help end domestic violence in our communities.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Bapa Sepanjang Hayat also organises talent competition shows with Keat Hong Community Centre where fathers take to the stage with their children, and showcase their singing and musical talents together.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What I find most touching was how they struggled and ultimately bonded in the journey during the preparation and audition for the competition.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Sixthly, proper planning and communication within families on sharing of duties and responsibilities on parenting.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Lastly, increased support through engagement and resources provided in the community for fathers.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It aims to support Singaporeans in starting and raising families.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: When she first suggested that we move this Motion together, I readily supported it because I believe that parents play a crucial role in their children's education, especially the involvement of fathers in their children's lives.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With the Government's family-friendly policies in all aspects of family life, such as education, housing and childcare, we can provide an environment that will better enable and support our young couples to start families and have children.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is crucial in order to build the next generation that can continue to strive for the overall prosperity and progress of our nation.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We have a large number of young parents in Keat Hong.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many couples are both working and at the same time, they strive hard to raise children who are still in school.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: During my house visits and interactions at preschool events in Keat Hong, I heard their concerns about the challenges of raising young children.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There are also some young couples without children who are worried about the cost of supporting and raising children in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In fact, in Keat Hong, I met many multi-generational families, where the elderly parents lamented that their grown-up children have settled down, but are not ready to have children.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Thus, they did not yet have the chance to cuddle a grandchild and be called "grandfather" or "grandmother".

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As for our young couples, they are worried about the challenges of starting a family and educating and raising children.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I want to dispel the notion that raising children is only about money.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Instead, it involves establishing a comprehensive ecosystem, which includes childcare in nurseries or kindergartens, a home environment that is conducive to family life, a family-friendly workplace and also parenting support and guidance for our families.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this respect, the Government's M3 initiative has reached out to many young couples via the Bersamamu programme and through the Matematika classes, which help parents and their preschool children prepare for primary school.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In fact, MENDAKI’s tuition classes provide high quality and very affordable tuition for our children.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Thus, there are various ways to manage the costs involved in supporting families and educating children, aside from the various Baby Bonus, subsidies, and tax rebates provided by the Government.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Apart from Government policies, we need initiatives that involve all parties, not just women, but men as well.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, the involvement of fathers in raising their children is not only beneficial for the child and family, but also for society as a whole.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Every year in Keat Hong, we organise various programmes to support fathers in their parenting journey, in collaboration with Government agencies and community partners.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, at M³@Chua Chu Kang, we have a series of programmes under the "Nakhoda Bahtera", or Ship Captain, initiative, touching on issues related to men and fathers, like leadership, parenting and men's health.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We also organise bowling events with fathers through Dads for Life and talent time competitions.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As Malay/Muslims, we also believe that children are not just a sacred trust bestowed upon us, but they are also a divine gift that brings blessings and prosperity for the family.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, I call upon all young couples to cherish every aspect of marriage and raising children.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As for the fathers, your sacrifices can never be fully repaid, but the reward will be apparent when the child that you raised and educated becomes a valuable and worthy individual in the eyes of society and the world, which is a testament of the efforts taken and to you who raised the child.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A verse of pantun or Malay quatrain: On the mountain, taro grows Tigers and deer, its slopes they climb A father's love forever flows Endlessly through the stream of time : Mr Speaker, Sir, fathers' involvement in child-raising is not only beneficial for children and families, but also for society as a whole.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, we fathers suffer sometimes what is called "dad guilt" in our experience in fatherhood.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We may be too busy with our careers, balancing between duties and responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My work as a disputes lawyer in international arbitration and my pro bono work in the community space meant that I am often travelling and takes me away from home.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My eldest daughter, when she was very young, was very often curious what I do.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Whenever I leave for my pro bono work, she will ask me, "Ayah, where are you going?" I did not have time to go into the details.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, I would just say, "I am going to help some people." This went on for a few occasions.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And then, one day, she stopped me at the door and asked me again, "Ayah, where are you going?", and I replied again, "To help some people." And then, she said something to me which I remember to this day.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I realised that in all my busyness, I had neglected the attention to my child.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And on that day, I brought her and her young sisters – she was like six years old then – to Casa Raudah, a women and children shelter home at which I was volunteering, to see first-hand what I do away from home and what I do during that time that I am away from her.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: At the end of the day, she understood.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: She saw first-hand the other girls in the home and she said to me, "Ayah, help more people then." Just like how children want to be in our lives, we fathers must involve our children actively in our lives.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Specifically, it was just about three months ago when I shared my thoughts on paternity leave, Shared Parental Leave, FWAs, childcare leave provisions during the debate on the CDCA Bill in November last year.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: At the risk of repeating myself ad nauseam, let me briefly recap some of the key points on these specific policy measures that I have been raising not just as a Member of Parliament reflecting the views of our residents, but also my personal experience as a father of two young boys, trying to raise a family in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To begin with, the Motion before us seeks to calls for the continued review and updating of policies to better support families, as well as the marriage and parenthood aspirations of Singaporeans, and endorses a whole-of-society approach to build a "Singapore Made for Families".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And we cannot expect incremental efforts to result in extraordinary results, if we do not make a serious effort to reimagine our approach to tackling this issue.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Three years on after the "A Singapore Made for Families 2025" plan was announced back in 2022, have we truly changed the status quo?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: On specific policy measures, let me first start by reiterating the point on FWAs, which I have spoken about on numerous occasions in this House.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Tripartite Guidelines for Flexible Work Arrangement Requests, which came into effect back in December, stipulates that employers must consider employees' requests for FWAs "properly".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Crucially, it stops short of legislating the right to request for FWAs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Ironically, despite the implementation of the Tripartite Guidelines in December, Blackbox Research's head of strategy expects to see a continued gradual decline in remote and hybrid working in 2025.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even in the United States (US), President Donald Trump has basically signed an executive order demanding all federal employees end their remote work arrangements and return to the office on a full-time basis or lose their jobs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This would make it easier for parents to care for their children whilst managing their work commitments.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: FWAs are also important in the context of our current childcare leave provisions.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If we cannot legislate for FWAs, can we then at least ensure that parents are able to care for the needs of their child via increasing the number of days of childcare leave, or to have it on a per-child basis?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In my speech in November last year, I shared that parents would need to care for their young children whenever their preschool closes, which according to ECDA, could be up to eight working days a year, an increase from six days a year previously.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I acknowledge that I had misspoken on this and Minister of State Sun Xueling clarified in her closing speech that there has been a net increase of only 0.5 days of preschool closure and not two additional days, as all preschools were already allowed to close 7.5 days per year – six closure days and three half-days on the eves of selected public holidays.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Does this not further prove my point that the existing childcare leave days are not even sufficient to cover for school closure days, let alone when our children fall sick?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, it seems that many preschools now have eight designated closure days and still have half-day closures on the eves of selected public holidays, anyway.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even though Minister of State Sun further shared that a working couple would have a total of 12 days of childcare leave on top of their annual leave provisions, are we not splitting hairs a little here?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yes, the manpower and operational needs of employers need to be taken into consideration, but should increasing the statutory childcare leave entitlements be deemed as having a substantial adverse effect on businesses, then perhaps, FWAs that parents can actually have could present itself as a viable solution.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Beyond the provision of FWAs and childcare leave, let us also take a moment to examine the lived realities of young Singaporean families: searching for a job in an increasingly hyper-competitive market; giving up personal passions and resigning to the corporate work grind to earn a living; stressing about the rising cost of living; facing the demands of returning to work and juggling parenthood throughout the child's early years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The physical, emotional and mental toll of a society where parents are hard at work is very real.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Feeling like your job or future career is at risk if one chooses to prioritise caregiving in the early years of parenthood is very real.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The survey also highlights the trend of reluctance and disinterest among young women's views on marriage and parenthood, where respondents are worried about burning out from juggling caregiving responsibilities and work demands, without equal support from their partners.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Individual choice aside, this is a society that places much higher emphasis on work over family.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We are also often reminded in this House, by the Government and some Members of Parliament (MPs), of the pushback from employers whenever we try to do better for our families, such as the impact of the parental leave enhancements on businesses and their manpower arrangements.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Adults of working age, including young Singaporeans parents or parents-to-be, are viewed as labour contributing to the output of this economy.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A parent that chooses to prioritise caregiving over a return to the workforce is an economic trade-off for Singapore, a role that does not contribute to gross domestic product (GDP).

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Our hyper-competitive economy pressures and expects new parents to return to the workforce, to pursue career growth and maximise earnings in a cycle where Singaporeans need to increase their earning ability in order to maintain living standards in an environment of rising costs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The measures we have today revolve heavily around financial support.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Besides the enhanced parental leave provision and infant care leave, this includes Baby Bonuses, Government contributions to child development accounts, child relief and childcare subsidies for working mothers and foreign domestic worker levy relief, again for working mothers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I recognise that these have provided significant relief and helped many Singaporeans build and raise families over the years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, we also know that generations of Singaporean children were primarily cared for through a mix of grandparents, domestic helpers and professional childcare, as their parents from the baby boomer generation generally prioritised work to earn a decent living.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even for myself, I cannot imagine how my family can cope without a combination of help from full-day childcare, a domestic helper and my mother-in-law.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We recognise that raising and nurturing a family is a lifelong journey, taking love, time and continual effort.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Being a parent and caring for your child is a privilege and responsibility.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, the existing frame does not seem to encourage this.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Instead, it prioritises the outsourcing of caregiving and incentivising parents, especially mothers, to return back to the workforce quickly.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: MSF's Social Compact wants families to be pillars of support and for families to be individually responsible.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, there is a fundamental disjunct between this and parents not having time or being empowered to prioritise childcare responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: When we provide childcare subsidies, tax reliefs and foreign domestic worker levy reliefs for working mothers only, we are saying, "We want you back in the workforce".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While this is ultimately dependent on parents' individual choice and we want to ensure that mothers are fully empowered to take charge of their own careers, parents should feel that they are empowered to make a choice to prioritise caregiving in the early years if they choose to do so.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If we truly believe in a "Singapore Made for Families", we need to expand and shift our frame from one that advocates for parents to outsource caregiving starting from as young as two months for infant care due to return to work demands, to a frame that champions parenthood.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We should be saying, "We want you to be proud of being a parent", and how we can rethink flexibility at work in the critical first years of a child growing up, so that parents are able to dedicate more time to directly care for their children.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Allow me now to say a few words in Mandarin, Sir.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: (In Mandarin):   Today’s Motion calls for the continued review and updating of policies to better support families, as well as the marriage and parenthood aspirations of Singaporeans, and endorses a whole-of-society approach to build a "Singapore Made for Families".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To achieve extraordinary results, we must make greater efforts and reimagine our approach.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Searching for a job in an increasingly hyper-competitive market.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Giving up personal passions and resigning to the corporate work grind to earn a living.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Facing the demands of returning to work and juggling parenthood throughout the child’s early years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: These are real predicaments that many parents are facing.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Financial and caregiving support incentives help, but if we are to truly build a "Singapore Made for Families", we need to rethink our starting point and reimagine our policies.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We must reimagine the intangible value of caregiving, challenging the emphasis of work over family and championing parenthood.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: That is the question we should be pondering. : Mr Speaker, beyond policies, we need to question the value that we place on work and the economy against that of parenthood and caregiving.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A "Singapore Made for Families" should be one where parents should not suffer from job insecurity because they choose to extend parental leave or prioritise caregiving during their child's formative years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Financial and caregiving support incentives help, but if we are to truly build a "Singapore Made for Families", we need to rethink our starting point and re-imagine our policies.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Re-imagining the intangible value of caregiving, challenging the emphasis of work over family and championing parenthood.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: That is the question we should be pondering.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: While I understand the context of his speech, but it is not clear from his speech whether he is in support of my Motion.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: So, I want to take this opportunity to seek his confirmation on that.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: Because I perceive that he is supporting my Motion, based on what I heard, especially in his Chinese speech, but I wish to seek his confirmation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Last year, Elon Musk declared that Singapore is going extinct with our low birth rate.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We do not need Elon Musk to point out that our low birth rate is a problem.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Progress Singapore Party (PSP) stands firm behind families and family values.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We understand that many Singaporeans desire to get married and have children, and we support these aspirations.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, it is ultimately a personal decision whether to get married and have children, and we respect these decisions too.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Women are not duty bound to have children and neither should singles be ashamed or treated differently because they are not married.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have a quote on my Facebook page since I entered politics in 2020, "Politics decide how a society looks like and society conditions what a person can do or cannot do.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We seek to establish the right kind of politics in our country so that all Singaporeans can perform to his full potential." I believe that each person makes the best possible life decisions for himself or herself under the socio-economic circumstances created by the Government and the society.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Accordingly, I also believe that the low TFR we see today is a result of the socio-economic circumstances that have been created by our Government's policies over the years.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP believes that this shows that these policies are not enough to resolve deeper societal issues that are discouraging Singaporeans from having children.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We strongly believe that the Government should not continue to rely on immigration as a solution to our nation's low TFR.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Instead, we have a duty to create conditions of economic and financial security so that Singaporeans can be optimistic about the future and feel confident about raising a child and build a society that is conducive for Singaporeans to start and raise families.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Older Members of this House will recall that during the 1980s and 1990s, good job opportunities were plentiful in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: HDB flat prices were affordable even for single income families.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There was strong wage growth. "明天会更好" or "Tomorrow Will Be Better", was a popular Chinese song in the late 1980s.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It was common to have two children or even three children and we were confident that our children will have better lives than us.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Today, with the rise of the gig economy, falling wage growth and resale HDB prices increasing faster than wages, Singaporeans are worried about their financial security.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many Singaporeans look at the million-dollar HDB flats in almost every town and wonder whether their children will be able to afford a decently sized HDB flat in the future.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The majority of married couples need dual incomes to afford the cost of living in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many young Singaporeans are also very worried about the impact of climate change.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many Singaporeans no longer have the confidence that the next generation would have better lives than ours.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP believes that we need to reset and re-imagine our socio-economic policies so that we can bring back confidence in the future.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have previously proposed many alternative policies in this House with that aim and we will do so again today.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have spoken extensively about rebalancing our foreign manpower policies to create better opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Family formation will be delayed if our university and polytechnic graduates are taking longer to find well-paying permanent jobs and also finding it harder to keep these jobs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need better policies to improve the job security of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While the Government has put in many measures since the loss of Aljunied Group Representation Constituency (GRC) in 2011, such as Fair Consideration Framework, the Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices (TAFEP), Complementarity Assessment Framework (COMPASS) and adjustments to the minimum qualifying salary, many Singaporeans are still concerned about job security.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We will not be able to increase TFR without allaying the concerns of Singaporeans about job security and work-life balance.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP has also proposed the Millennial Apartments Scheme, which aims to provide young Singaporeans with a quality rental option while they are waiting for a new flat.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are confident that these two schemes, taken together, will reduce the cost of housing for Singaporeans and allow young Singaporeans to get their own home as quickly as possible once they are ready to set up a family.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thirdly, we must further defray the cost of prenatal gynaecologist visits, childbirth and postpartum medical checks.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP believes that maternity and child-bearing medical fees should be fully claimable from MediSave without limit.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Given our low TFR, there is little concern about overusing MediSave for such fees.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Female Singaporeans should have full autonomy over how much MediSave they want to use.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Most mothers in Singapore, regardless of race, also practice confinement, which helps the mother heal physically from childbirth and adjust to a life with a newborn, which can be very challenging and even lead to postpartum depression for some mothers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But with basic confinement packages at $3,000 to $5,000 now, the cost of confinement care can be expensive.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Fourth, we must strengthen workplace support for caregiving of children.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP acknowledges that the Government has put in place a wide range of support programmes for parents and introduced new forms of support, such as paternity leave.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, to allow parents to spend more quality time with their children and enjoy parenting, we should have bolder policies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should create conditions such that Singaporean families can thrive with just one-and-a-half income instead of two incomes.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This means that families should be able to afford the cost of living with one full-time working parent and another parent working flexi-time.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this regard, we can do more to encourage job-sharing and the adoption of FWAs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government has introduced the job-sharing incentive to support companies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In creating FWAs or job-sharing arrangements for their employees.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Under the current scheme, each company receives up to $35,000, depending on the number of employees that have adopted FWAs or job-sharing.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We hope that this will incentivise more employers to create flexi-time jobs and help workers to better balance their work and family commitment.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Fifth, we should recognise the great unpaid contributions of homemakers and full-time caregivers of young children.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many parents, especially mothers, choose to sacrifice their careers to bring up their children.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Grandparents also help full-time working parents with caregiving duties and bringing the grandchildren to school, minding them after school and cooking for them.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I first mentioned such a monthly allowance in my Budget speech in 2023.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Those who claim this allowance would no longer be eligible for Government subsidies for full-day childcare and infant care programmes.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Part-time care caregivers or babysitters, like myself, would also not qualify.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This allowance is expected to be a game-changer, as it will provide real and effective support for full-time homemakers and caregivers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our sixth and last policy suggestion is to reduce education pressure on families to promote happier family lives.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Most preschoolers are sent to tuition or expensive kindergartens to get a head start in life.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This kind of pressure is taking a toll on young children and we cannot afford the negative effects it has on their mental health.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have heard many young Singaporeans who are choosing not to have children because they do not want them to face this kind of suffering.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To encourage more Singaporeans to have children, we must do more to reduce the pressures currently faced by the young in our education system.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We reiterate our suggestion to offer an option of not having to take the PSLE.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Members of the House from all parties have made this suggestion before.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will allow children to be happier and parents to enjoy happier family lives.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Let us imagine how enjoyable family life in Singapore would be if Singaporeans have stable jobs, can afford the cost of living with one-and-a-half incomes, can easily get a house to form a family whenever they are ready and can spend quality time with children who are free from exam pressures.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Grandparents can spend time taking care of their grandchildren with a caregiving allowance from the Government, instead of working in old age.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am confident that more Singaporeans will be willing to have children if we can create such an environment for families.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The low TFR is an existential problem which should be tackled as a national emergency.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If our current birth rate persists, there will only be 12 great-grandchildren for every Singaporeans born today.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is little point in increasing the Reserves if we do not have a future generation to leave the Reserves to.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should use our hard-earned savings to invest in our people and re-imagine our socio-economic policies, so that more Singaporeans will consider parenthood a meaningful and attainable journey.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We already know that these policies are ineffective and that is why, we are facing a national emergency today.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What we urgently need, is to re-imagine some new policies and mobilise the whole of Government, and whole of society, to create an environment that is conducive for families and raising children.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP has provided some new ideas as a starting point and hope that this will develop into a national action plan.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As such, Mr Speaker, may I seek your permission to move an amendment to the Motion.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Yes, please let me have a copy of the amendment.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Okay, the amendment submitted by Mr Leong Mun Wai is in order.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Not everyone may agree with our new ideas, but we hope that Members will agree that we need new ideas to better support families.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It may be convenient that the debate on the original Motion and on any other amendments moved by Members be proceeded with simultaneously as a debate on a single question.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Do I have hon Members' agreement to this?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This phrase means that families, as the smallest units in a society, play an important role and have an impact in shaping values and strengthening any society.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Therefore, Sir, when there are efforts that help improve family life, such efforts are very much welcome and must be given full support.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: My colleagues and I from the Workers' Party have given various suggestions as well as underlined the importance of having more family-friendly government schemes and policies, coupled with less pressure and more happiness, in order to further improve family life in Singapore, which will thereby further strengthen Singaporean families, thus forming a more prosperous, strong and cohesive society.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I have done so during my first term.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In addition, I have, on many occasions, raised in this House the concerns and grievances of segments of Singaporeans who are still burdened with challenges and hardships of family life that made them feel marginalised and neglected.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In today's debate, I would like to once again focus on two groups of Singaporean families facing challenges, in the hope that their concerns and feedback will receive due attention.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Due to this concern, these individuals who are about to become single parents will apply to get rental flats under the Public Rental Scheme.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Usually, for such cases, HDB will tell the applicants to wait until their divorce case is settled in order for it to be evaluated and processed.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I acknowledge that HDB will do its best when considering applications and appeals from these soon-to-be single parents.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, I feel that the existing system or process can still be improved and refined.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This will at least provide some form of assurance to the applicants and also can alleviate the pressure that they face.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: At the same time, this proposed process can reduce the waiting time to get rental flats for these applicants.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: More importantly, a more in-depth and thorough evaluation process like this can address situations where cases are overlooked or had "fallen through the cracks".

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This group often laments that they cannot live together as a family because they are often separated due to their inability to obtain LTVPs for their partners and other family members.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: There are also reports of couples who are burdened with this challenge and had to divorce due to the intense pressure of having to always live separately because they were unable to obtain LTVPs.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, at the same time, I do wonder how an applicant would be able to fulfil the factors set out by ICA?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This situation is akin to the question "which comes first, the chicken or egg?".

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: How would ICA be able to assess factors like economic contributions, length of residency, the applicant’s ability to contribute to Singapore and integrate in our society, as well as the applicant’s commitment to sink roots, as stated in ICA’s website, when the applicants themselves have little chance to try and fulfil those factors because they are in Singapore for a limited time as short-term visit pass holders?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I believe that this approach may be insufficient to obtain a comprehensive assessment of the problems or challenges that are faced by those submitting appeals for rejected applications.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This will potentially increase household income and therefore alleviate any financial burden.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: For elderly applicants requiring care, in addition to their partners having the opportunity to work and increase their income, the presence of their partners by their side for an extended period is very much needed, to provide companionship in their twilight years, and for those who have health issues, their partners can be there and provide the best care.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I had the joy of growing up in a big extended family.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My parents' HDB flat was near my aunt's flat and my grandmother's HDB shophouse, where other uncles and aunties lived in.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I had a very happy childhood, playing with my cousins every day after school, as my mom and aunties would help in my grandmother's shop and the children would congregate there after school for homework and play, before returning to our respective homes each night.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I grew up thinking that everyone has a family like mine and will desire such a family like mine.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For this speech, I checked and noted that the Singapore's TFR was 2.98 when I was born in 1972.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To prepare for this speech, I interviewed four groups of my Jalan Kayu residents and personal friends: first, singles who desire to marry but have not found the right person to marry yet; second, singles who desire to marry and have found the right person but have not married yet; third, young married couples who desire children but have none yet; and fourthly, young married couples who desire children and have them.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: According to the findings of the IPS pre-conference poll shared at the Singapore Perspectives Conference in January 2024, young Singaporeans are less likely to think it is necessary to marry and have children, but most still aspire to do so.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The survey was done to get a sense of Singaporeans' attitudes and views towards issues like family, well-being and work.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It found that our young Singaporeans are experiencing higher levels of loneliness.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A representative sample of about 2,400 Singapore residents were also polled by IPS between November and December 2023 in three age groups: the youngest, 21- to 34-year-olds; the middle, 35- to 49-year-olds; and the older, 50- to 64-year-olds.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Across all age groups, the top two reasons for not dating or getting married are that they have not met the right person yet and that they prefer to remain single.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although there has been a growing acceptance for online dating apps, 80% of the surveyed respondents prefer meeting potential partners through more organic and face-to-face settings.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I suggested then that a community approach may be more suitable for the Government to encourage more organic social mingling and urged the Government to be open to investing more to help singles expand their social circle and actively encourage our singles to mingle in social settings.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Armed with the survey data and my experience when I was a civil servant in the Ministry of Health's (MOH's) Office for Healthcare Transformation in piloting projects to achieve proof of concept and proof of value outcomes in hopes that the Government will consider mainstream funding support, I went about researching what I could pilot for my Jalan Kayu young residents.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Around then, I met Friendzone SG at an April 2023 conversation session for young people in Jalan Kayu funded by the Ministry of Digital Development and Information's (MDDI's) Reaching Everyone for Active Citizenry @ Home (REACH) department.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Friendzone is a ground-up social enterprise started in 2018 by a young Singaporean who believes in building friendships, teams and communities one conversation at a time.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Remembering how my own marriage, which reached its 21st anniversary last Friday, was built on the foundation of friendship, I thought that would be a good starting point and connected Friendzone to my young leaders in Jalan Kayu Youth Network (YN) to explore collaborations.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Knowing that as a social enterprise, Friendzone needed funding for materials and time to carefully plan, outreach and facilitate each conversation session, I raised the matter with our Jalan Kayu Citizen Consultative Committee.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I was touched by the swift and unanimous support from long-serving grassroots leaders, many in their 50s and 60s, who readily agreed to utilising our Citizen Consultative Committee funds to pilot two Friendzone sessions.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our resourceful Jalan Kayu YN further stretched the Citizen Consultative Committee budget to do four sessions, from 2023 to 2024, by negotiating for discounted grassroot rates and collaborating with other YNs in Ang Mo Kio GRC, sourcing for National Youth Council's (NYC's) inter-generation engagement grants, People's Association (PA) GRC dialogue grants for youth and co-funding with other YNs to do more sessions for more young people to benefit.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One of the four sessions was on 7 July 2024 at our annual Jalan Kayu Day last year, where Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong was the guest-of-honour and interacted with our young residents at the Friendzone conversations on the topic of friendship and relationships.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My hope is that the Government can consider one stream of funding support for every constituency to be able to conduct such sessions, without each MP, like me, having to worry about raising funds to start and sustain the platform.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our YNs can also focus on organising such collaborations and outreach rather than navigating different Government grants to carry out what they find useful.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: JK Y-Connect will facilitate learning on topics, such as dating etiquettes, healthy dating mindset and behaviours, positive ways to find the "right partner" through self-discovery and discovery of potential partners in a fun, unintimidating and authentic way.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that Jalan Kayu young residents can have Friendzone-type of platforms to just make friends over conversations and topics of their interest, as well as the upcoming Y-Connect for those who would like to explore more dating.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Next, for my residents who are single, desire to marry and have found the right person but have not yet married.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The IPS pre-conference poll in January 2024, which I cited earlier, also identified cost of living as the top of the list of social issues that young Singaporeans are most concerned about.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Several of my young residents who fall into this group shared with me that they are still saving up for their dream wedding as hotel banquet costs have risen substantially post-COVID-19 pandemic and partially due to global geopolitical and economic factors, which are beyond their controls and they feel somewhat helpless about.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When I visited Seoul in 2013 on a study trip while I was a public servant in the National Council of Social Service, I was impressed by a briefing from the equivalent of our MSF on an idea initiated by their Mayor Oh Se-Hoon, who was first elected in 2006 and is the incumbent Seoul Mayor today.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The initiative was to open a new, state-of-the-art architecture designed and built city hall, with a large basement comprising a citizen's plaza, a gallery, an exhibition hall and an event hall for booking and use by Seoul citizens for diverse purposes.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To commemorate the opening of this new city hall in a special way then, the city of Seoul's government hosted a "First New City Hall Wedding" call.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The bride and groom would be required to receive premarital education before the wedding.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The "First New City Hall Wedding" call also offered several talented local professionals who donated their services, including a master of ceremony, congratulatory singers, photographers and so on.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The couple could also receive assistance from a socially responsible wedding company consigned by the government agency.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, it is up to the couple to use the wedding company at their own cost.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: After this unusual call to commemorate the opening of the new city hall, which saw overwhelming applications, the Seoul government continued to make the event hall available for wedding ceremonies weekly for Seoul citizens.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For those curious, I assure you that the event hall was nothing short of a dream wedding venue that are alike those seen in many beautiful K-drama weddings, when I visited in 2013.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope for a chance to visit again when I travel to Seoul.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am sure that cost-conscious young Singaporeans with a hope for a dream wedding, alike any young couples around the world, will appreciate a similar programme to make their wedding plans less of a financial burden, but more of a real bliss.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Moving on to the group of young married couples who desire children but have not had any yet.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The representative 2023 poll by IPS, which I mentioned earlier, also saw 67% of the youngest respondents, between 21 and 34, without children hoping to have kids.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A researcher in that poll said that the young worry about the cost of housing.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: High cost and stress emerged as the top reasons for not wanting to have children across all age groups.
