speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While the number of young married couples still waiting for a successful ballot for a new, affordable BTO flat, whom I see at my weekly MPS has eased from the high number during and right after the COVID-19 pandemic crunch, I empathise with these young couples who are still disappointed to get no queue number or a queue number far exceeding the available units in each BTO or Sales of Balance flats application exercise.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The hybrid system can help not to delay their obtaining of a new flat much longer, in both non-mature and mature estates.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For mature estates, there can be additional criteria, like proximity to parents or parent-in-laws who have been living in the mature estate for a considerable number of years and the young couples are looking to them for childcare support or need to care for their ageing parents.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Lastly, I had the joy of interviewing two couples in their mid-30s to early-40s, with four children each.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I shared with them that they are defying the odds of shrinking family sizes and falling TFR, experienced not just in Singapore but in all major highly-developed urban cities and countries.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I asked them what their "secret sauces" are.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Each one stepping up and stepping down in career pursuits and other life aspirations over the course of achieving a common goal of building a big, happy family filled with laughers and, many times, cries of children.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It reminds me of a Bible verse, Ecclesiastes 4:9-12: "Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their toil.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For if they fall, one will lift the other.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Again, if two lie together, they keep warm." Even when I started drafting this speech on the second day of Chinese New Year, a young friend happily announced to me the arrival of his third child, a beautiful daughter named Caroline, which filled me with such joy and inspirations to complete this speech while shuttling from house visits for Chinese New Year and events with family and residents.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Back in English, the phrase means a home thrives on the foundation of a good country, and one thrives on the foundation of a good home.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It gives me hope for this homeland, this nation, this Singapore, that we all love and the people in this land who are the most precious, both when we first achieved Independence in 1965, as it is today in 2025, as we celebrate SG60 as one nation and one people.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As we celebrate SG60 with pride and new hopes, surely, the best is yet to come with daughters and sons of a better age in writing new history and uplifting records, including our TFR, for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have recently been blessed with the chance to become a mother and the arrival of our little boy has brought new perspectives as well as solidified previous beliefs.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One such belief is from the old phrase, "It takes a village to raise a child." I would like to take a moment to express my deep respect and appreciation for all parents and caregivers who raise children; from infant carers and early childhood educators who look after children when mummies and daddies go to work; foreign domestic workers who share the load of keeping a home neat and tidy; grandparents who go through a sequel of raising the grandchildren later in life; friends who happily babysit our children for a few hours; well-wishers who offer encouraging words; doctors and nurses who bring them into this world and care for them when they are sick, it does indeed take a kampung and I am very grateful for mine.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is not our place to impose our personal preferences on others, but from a statistical perspective, encouraging more families to have children is indeed critical to Singapore's future.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The caregiving burden will grow, and in family units where there are single children, this typically falls upon them.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, this pressing need at the country level may not find resonance at a personal level with Singaporeans for many reasons.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Coming out of the Chinese New Year period, I am sure many around my age are asked some permutation of the famous trinity of questions.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And the third, no matter how recently you have given birth, when are you having a second one?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I answered the first question, "When are you getting married?", after I turned 28, just 1.5 years shy of the median age of first marriages in Singapore for brides in 2023.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For grooms, this is 31, also in line with the global trend of later marriages.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But peak fertility age is in the earlier part of our 20s.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For those who are graduating from Institutions of Higher Learning (IHLs), 20s is often a time of "chiong-ing", pursuing career, supporting older parents, saving up for that BTO.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For many, it is also the first time out of formal education, where the world seems less linear, opportunities abound and experiences like travel open up more.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, for many youths today, the picture of marriage and family where men go out to work and women stay at home to raise children is outdated and less enticing.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One of the principal investigators in Singapore, Prof Yong, said that "Singaporeans seem to think that women who work and do most of the domestic duties at home are not any worse off than if both husband and wife share the domestic duties equally when they are both in the workforce".

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Despite much progress over the years, women still find themselves carrying an unequal mental load and face bias in workplace and society, for example, in terms of sexist comments and being the default parent.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And so, a rising number of women choose to stay single, prioritising freedom and the ability to invest in their career, hobby and other pursuits.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While moves have been made in recent time to nudge equality in family life, for example, through Shared Parental Leave, ultimately, it will take time for mindsets to shift.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Society must also change its views on men who choose to stay home at work or work more flexible roles, appreciate those who are active fathers alongside their partners and give them space to participate meaningfully in the raising of children.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We are all responsible for the gender stories that we live and tell, and these affect our social identities, from how we advertise to the way we value care work, how we interact with each other at home in terms of chores, careless stereotypes and how we speak to girls and boys from a young age.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Society must do better to challenge these stereotypes.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Which leads me to the second question, "When are you having a baby?" At our wedding, my husband shared that how he knew we were right for each other was that it was the first time he could see himself starting a family.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I, too, could envision him, not just as a good husband, but as a great daddy.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Intentional and thoughtful about the kind of values we would hope to impart to our kids, but also aware of just how much it takes to try and raise them accordingly.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But for six years, as much as we wanted, we could not answer the second question, for a variety of personal reasons.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Every year which passed would see more questions, reinforced this time with "don't wait so long" and "you're not getting any younger, you know".

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As I neared 35, the reminder that my biological clock was ticking loomed over me, as did reminders that I was born with a fixed number of eggs, which were depleting, both in quality and quantity, as the months went by.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While some may choose to stay single or childfree, not enough is said for those who long for children of their own but are unable to become a parent.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This could be due to health reasons, whether physical or mental, anxieties or traumas from their own childhood, a lack of information or a lack of financial resources to seek help early.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While questions often focus on the woman, causes of infertility are actually relatively split evenly between male and female factors.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is one thing to encourage people to have children, but even more important for people to be empowered with information to make their own informed decisions.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These topics can also be included as part of marriage preparation programmes, such that young couples can discuss things like fertility screening, having children and financial considerations early.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Female and male infertility can be a sensitive issue and it would be helpful for couples to have the option of facilitated discussions by experts.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Fertility treatments can also be taxing both emotionally and financially.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While elective egg freezing is not a guarantee for babies later in life.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am glad that we have moved on permitting this as of 2023, including raising the age limit from 35 to 37, so as to cater for women to have more options.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Beyond that, there is also the time off from work required, the check-up, the injections, the careful counting, the restrictions on diet and lifestyle.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My favourite is the advice "try not to stress" in an already very stressful situation.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To quote a Reddit user, egg freezing is an amazing innovation, but it is so far from cost free.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am glad that we are doing more to help Singaporeans fulfil their dreams of having children for those who choose to do so and hope that more will come forward to support each other on this journey.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To this end, I am grateful for platforms such as Fertility SG, a non-profit started by IVF warriors, which provides a safe space for men and women who wish to find out more about fertility health and assisted reproduction.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is important that this information and support is available to people from all walks of life.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Modern parenting can be overwhelming with society's expectations and our own, from Instagram posts on expensive gender reveal parties, pregnancy and baby photo shoots, breastfeeding, milk supply woes, the never-ending list of things to purchase for our little ones, to advice from well-meaning strangers.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have read cases of postpartum depression affecting marriages and cases which have also ended in the tragic loss of life.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It could be helpful if there was an automated process where parents receive an email or SMS after registering their child's birth or before leaving the hospital, where parents could consider and consent to have their contact information shared so as to join community circles near their homes, perhaps at the nearest community club or other organisations.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hospitals can also provide bite size information to spot signs of postnatal depression via text if parents consent; and this can also be provided upon discharge after delivery.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Over the last few years, I have come across residents who have tried very hard to start their own journey into familyhood, or who wish to grow their families but housing remains a challenge.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For many, the desire to have a home starts from having a house.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Even though the Government has introduced a slew of measures, such as first-timer priority and the family and parenthood priority scheme, for those who live in estates such as Ang Mo Kio, new sales launches are few and far between due to the lack of land parcels to build on.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Young residents who have lived here all their life often lament the inability to secure housing near their parents who they wish to stay near to for caregiving purposes.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For longevity, couples also tend to prefer at least a 4-room flat to cater for a bedroom for themselves, a combination of one or two children, a caregiver, such as a helper or their parents, and living space to cater to work-from-home arrangements.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While resale flats are an option, a quick search on the HDB website of resale flat prices in the last six months in Ang Mo Kio for 4-room flats range from $455,000 to above $1 million.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I recognise that the Government has taken steps to cool the market and that this is, ultimately, a case of "willing buyer, willing seller", but this can be very daunting for young couples.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Also, given that grandparents often play an important caregiving role in raising children, could the Government also consider building more 3Gen units in such towns so that families have the option of staying together under one roof?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While this also means that redevelopment into potential new BTO housing is halted, for example, in the case of Tanglin Halt, I know that many are relieved that they are able to secure this interim housing while awaiting their keys.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While many understand this, a young couple shared with me their disappointment in failing to secure a unit despite multiple applications.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although they are married, they continue to live separately with their respective parents due to space constraints and the expensive private rental market.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This too, can be a barrier to starting a family.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Success for me has been redefined somewhat and can be as simple as having 10 minutes in between work to hold him and feed him, or watching him interact with his daddy and his grandparents.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As we build a "Singapore Made for Families", I am grateful that we already have several of the key building blocks in place: safe streets, well planned towns, with homes and with childcare options, decisive shifts on paid parental leave, good education system and more.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must continue to support families of all shapes and sizes, to assure Singaporeans that the Government and society at large will walk alongside them in this journey.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To tie my speech back to Chinese New Year, amidst the well wishes of 早生贵子, or may you be blessed with a child soon, I wish you strength, patient and hope your hearts find peace.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP absolutely agrees that a whole-of-society approach is needed to build a Singapore that is made for families.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, PSP believes that without new policy ideas or major policy shifts, we will not be able to adequately support the marriage and parenthood aspirations of Singaporeans, or reverse or stabilise the decline in TFR that we have seen over the last few decades.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That is why we have raised an amendment to the Motion today to call for a re-imagination of the current policies which, in our view, have not been enough.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For those who do not wish to have children, we should respect their personal choice.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But for those who wish to have children, there are things the Government can do to lower the barriers and reduce the obstacles in their way.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One key concern of potential parents is the cost of raising children.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If our young people are struggling with the cost of living, it will dissuade them from having children which will further add to their financial burden.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Young people are naturally concerned about whether having children would affect their jobs and career progression.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My colleague, Mr Leong Mun Wai, has already spoken about job-sharing.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I will speak on improving the attitude of employers towards their employees having children.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For employers, their manpower situation is adversely impacted when employees take maternity or paternity leave.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is, therefore, a potential conflict in the interest of society and the interest of employers.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need to implement measures to instead align the interest of employers to the interest of society.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP urges the Government to introduce incentives for employers with family-friendly policies and environment.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While we exercise control over our dependence on foreign manpower at the national level, we can tilt the balance towards family-friendly employers, by giving them relatively higher access to foreign manpower.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, one way is to give additional quota or COMPASS points.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the total parental leave taken by the employees is 30 weeks, then the employer can be entitled to the additional quota for 60 weeks, to more than compensate them for the loss in manpower.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Employers may be incentivised to introduce policies and environment for better work life balance so that their employees have more time and energy to socialise, meet their better halves, form families and carry out parental duties.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For Singaporeans to be more receptive to foreigners, Singaporeans must be able to see that the participation of foreigners in our economy improves their quality of life.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP has proposed the Affordable Homes Scheme to deal with the high cost of housing, but another key impediment to raising our TFR is the long waiting time for a HDB flat, as has also been pointed out by the hon Member, Ms Nadia Samdin, just now.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The waiting time under the BTO system plus the requirement to find a partner first before you can apply, can greatly delay Singaporeans' family formation.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Whilst the Government has started building flats with Shorter Waiting Time (SWT), the number of such flats at 2,000 to 4,000 units per year is way too low.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The number of citizen marriages in 2023 is over 24,000.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We urge the Government to more aggressively increase the supply of the SWT flats.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With young people prioritising career development and the long waiting time for housing, Singaporeans are getting married later and having children later.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These delays can result in fertility issues, compounding the problem.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The struggle with infertility is a personal one for me.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I tried to conceive naturally for 10 years after getting married to no avail.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I sought medical treatment after that, but my body reacted badly to the medications.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thus, my husband and I decided to turn to adoption.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It seems like yesterday when we brought our two sons home as infants, but they are already 18 and 17 now.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I therefore empathise deeply with couples who are struggling with infertility and going through assisted reproductive technologies (ART) treatments like IVF.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such treatments are often especially taxing for women, who may have to endure multiple rounds of medications, self-administered injections and hospital visits.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP believes that as a society, we can do more to support couples going through ART.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government co-funds a maximum of three fresh and three frozen ART cycles.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The last two co-funded cycles can be completed after age 40, as long as ART or intrauterine insemination procedures have been attempted before age 40.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Israel is the only Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) country that is still reproducing above the replacement rate.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: An OECD report in 2024 found that it has a TFR of 2.9, with Mexico and France in second place at 1.8.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Part of this is due to religious reasons as the ultra-Orthodox Jewish community have many children.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But even secular women in Israel have a TFR of 2.0.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is believed that part of the reason behind this is strong state support for assisted reproduction.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is estimated that at least 2% of the Israeli health budget goes towards funding IVF treatments.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is in stark contrast to our funding policies, which only provides up to 75% co-funding, with stricter age limits and co-funding limits based on the citizenship status of couples and the number of ART cycles.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Currently, only couples where both spouses are Singapore Citizens are eligible to receive the full 75% co-funding for assisted conception procedures.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government will only co-fund 55% if one spouse is a PR and 35% if one spouse is a foreigner.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Trans-national marriages now make up 36% of citizen marriages, as of 2023.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, PSP believes that we can increase the number of ART cycles eligible for co-funding.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In a reply to a Parliamentary Question by Mr Louis Ng in January 2024, Minister Ong Ye Kung, said that the current co-funding limit of three fresh and three frozen ART cycles strikes a balance between providing public-funded financial support to couples aspiring to be parents and ensuring the prudent use of public funds by taking into account clinical efficacy.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But given that our fertility rates are currently extremely low, we should rethink our approach towards rationing ART cycles and move closer to an Israeli approach to funding.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Israeli experience suggests that this would be a worthwhile investment.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For women from age 40 to 45, we should co-fund three fresh and three frozen ART cycles.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This has extended to the Government's financial support for couples facing fertility issues.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we really hope to stop our TFR from declining, or reverse the decline, we should re-think the balance between fiscal prudence and supporting couples with fertility issues.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the Committee of Supply last year, I called on the Government to consider some level of subsidies in public hospitals and allow the use of MediSave for egg freezing.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such financial support is already being extended in countries overseas.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Conditions on subsidies can be imposed to prevent abuse.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Unutilised frozen eggs can be donated to other couples or used for other purposes like research or education.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In a Parliamentary Question reply yesterday, Minister Ong Ye Kung said that our financing policies for egg freezing are designed on clinical grounds and from a population policy perspective, the Government does not want to inadvertently encourage young couples to delay their plans.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our young people should be given the freedom to decide on their life choices, including marriage and parenthood, based on their own personal circumstances, not pushed into it before they are ready.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What we can do, is to provide an environment that can help them be ready earlier and support them in their efforts to become parents.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I urge the Government to reconsider our proposals.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Women who choose to go through the pain and discomfort of egg freezing demonstrate strong parenthood aspirations.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should do more to support them, even if it means doing something unprecedented with regard to our health policy.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, PSP believes that in the face of our country's continuous declining TFR over many years, it is not enough to merely continue reviewing and updating our policies to support Singaporeans' marriage and parenthood aspirations.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need to reimagine these policies to adequately support Singaporeans in building families and to reverse or stabilise the decades long trend of declining TFR.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Therefore, we are proposing an amendment to the Motion today.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For those who do not wish to have children, we should respect their personal choice.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, for those who wish to have children, the Government can take more measures to pave the way for them.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Today, Mr Leong Mun Wai and I reiterated PSP's proposals to reduce the cost of living and housing cost.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope all Members will support the amended Motion.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   Singapore's fertility rate has been low for a long time, which is a major problem that bothers us.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although the Government has taken many measures, there are still few results.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Instead, we should be determined and have the courage to continue to introduce more favourable measures to increase the fertility rate and change the declining trend in the birth rate.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Clearly, economic factors are still the main reason affecting fertility.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Therefore, I suggest providing all-round economic support at all stages of a child's development.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We can increase the parenthood subsidies, increase the quantum of Baby Bonus and expand it to more families, and increase childcare subsidies.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The cost of commercial childcare centres is very high and the Government should increase funding for them, improving their quality and reduce the cost of childcare for parents.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mencius once said, "For the order and stability of a country, it is necessary for its people to have a property of their own." We also pursue our home ownership policy in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I think the Government should create a housing policy that is more friendly to young couples.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We know that birds will build their nests before they lay eggs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Young couples who are about to become parents would always want to buy a house for their new family before considering having children.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It can be said that buying a house is a must for young couples!

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must take care of the housing needs of these young couples, give them higher priority in the queue, increase their housing subsidies, lower the threshold for home ownership and shorten the waiting time.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While waiting for a BTO flat, we can provide short-term subsidised rental flats for couples.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We can also give priority to families with more children to move to larger HDB flats first, exempt them from the Minimum Occupation Period (MOP) requirement and increase the number of subsidies. : Will HDB consider allowing couples to upgrade and exchange to bigger flats with more rooms when they have at least three babies, without requiring them to fulfil the MOP, and only need to top up the difference between their original purchase price and the bigger BTO flat upon exchange with HDB?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The bigger flat also takes into consideration the family's need to accommodate a helper or grandparents to take care of the young ones.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Next, the size of our flats may be a contributing factor to low fertility.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If we build more smaller flats based on the norm of smaller households, it may become an entrenched, self-fulfilling trend, where new households have fewer children to fit comfortably into the available flat sizes.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Government consider increasing the sizes of flats and the number of bigger flats with six rooms or more, and in tandem, increase the quantum of HDB subsidies with every child born, up to four children, specifically for the family with more than two children?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These subsides should be claimable with the birth of each qualified child.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must continue to expedite the building of HDB flats and the collection of keys.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should give allocation priority to first-timer couples, followed by families based on the number of children under the age of 18 in the household.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Declining fertility has been a challenging issue in many developed countries, even among those with generous Government support schemes, such as Sweden and Norway.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Nonetheless, we must persist with initiatives to create and maintain a conducive environment to encourage Singaporeans to have and raise children.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The assistance will ease the transition for the arrival of a new baby and nudge some parents to consider having more.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When the Prime Minister suggested more maternal and paternal leave, this was welcomed by couples but some also expressed concerns over the potential trade-offs, such as the loss of opportunities due to competition in jobs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some in the corporates have also expressed concerns over the sharing of heavier loads among colleagues that may not be rewarded.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On a positive note, it may also encourage employers to relook at the need to retain senior staff to give support to their colleagues with young family.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This could potentially be a win-win situation for the job market and employment.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need to factor in the growing trend of more singles across all age groups, with the most significant increase amongst those age 25 to 34.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For many of them, marriage is no longer as much of a priority, but they are open to marriage if they meet suitable partners, as was mentioned by some of the Members here.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We are also operating in an environment of greater caution due to the worrying number of scams, including on dating apps.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This framework could provide a safe and trusted space for busy singles to network and meet potential partners beyond their usual work and social circles.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Government may consider building confinement care facilities to support both parents and baby at subsidised and affordable rates in new towns and estates.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: More senior citizens today continue to work longer, some even past their retirement age.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It may be quite a financial loss to them to babysit their grandchildren.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: "Four seasons fill the measure of the year; there are four seasons in the mind of man." This excerpt from the poem "Sonnet.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The Human Seasons" by 19th century English poet John Keats, likens human life to the passage of the four seasons.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: As we transition from the spring of childhood into the summer of youth and graduate into the autumn of middle age and the winter of old age, many of us count on our families to be there for us.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: While family mattered most to Singaporeans, the same IPS study shared that work was a higher priority for Singaporeans aged between 36 and 50 than other age groups, likely because this group of Singaporeans tend to be breadwinners who feel responsible for their family’s finances, care and well-being.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The Motion calls for a Singapore social compact that can help these Singaporean breadwinners to balance the economics and emotions of working and caregiving, because doing so is integral to a "Singapore Made for Families".

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Then-Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong also gave similar assurances when he said at the launch of the Forward Singapore exercise in June 2022, that "Singaporeans and Singaporean workers will always be at the centre of everything we do." Such assurance matters because year 2025 is unfolding in a world that is increasingly driven by technology and often times delicate, uncontrollable, unpredictable and impossible to comprehend.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Allow me to share about three groups of Singaporean breadwinners who must show courage as they brave a new wave of technological disruption that could upend livelihoods and intensify the challenge in raising their families.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: What could be strengthened in our social compact so that these Singaporean workers can rise above new areas of adversity, challenge and uncertainty and be a pillar of strength and support for their families?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: During the debate on the Workplace Fairness Bill, I pointed out that some became platform workers because platform work allowed them to earn a living despite their limitations.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, some platform delivery members from the National Trade Unions Congress' (NTUC's) National Delivery Champions Association are single parents and the main caregivers to their young school-going children.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Because these platform delivery workers are careful to only accept platform jobs that they can fulfil when their children are at school, they worry that they could be deprioritised in job allocation and/or fares by biases learnt or internalised by platform algorithms.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Such action by the platform algorithms would hurt such platform workers' livelihoods and compel these workers to unfairly choose between work and caregiving.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: I would also like to continue urging the Government to consider requiring these AI-centric companies to adopt the Infocomm Media Development Authority's (IMDA's) AI Verify governance framework that would guide companies to be transparent about their AI and build trust.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Such moves would give greater assurance to breadwinners with precarious work, such as platform workers.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Nearly 70% of 4,000 global marketing and creative leaders, surveyed by Canva, a multinational graphic design platform, expressed concern over potential job loss across industries due to Generative AI (GenAI).

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: GenAI and globalisation are reshaping the nature of creative work in Singapore.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: NTUC's Visual, Audio and Creative Content Professionals Association that represents freelance creative professionals, observed that companies are becoming more cost-conscious and have increasingly delegated tedious time-consuming tasks, such as localising and personalising creative concepts for marketing campaigns to AI.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This is similar in concept to how the UK's government procurement framework requires government departments to consider social value in awarding contracts.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, departments are guided to consider social value outcomes that have lasting impact to individuals, communities and the environment, such as "tackling economic inequality, including creating new businesses, jobs and skills" as well as "driving equal opportunity".

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Likewise, having the Government take the lead in contracting and subcontracting Singaporean creatives for Government-commissioned projects would provide the safe space for these creative freelancers to apply new knowledge and technology that expand creative frontiers, capture new value and elevate the standing of Singaporean creatives.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Such move would pave the way for local creative freelancers to translate upskilling efforts into a differentiated creative portfolio.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: A differentiated creative portfolio matters because it can be a springboard for local freelance creatives to pitch beyond Singapore for higher value creative work and to command a premium for their expertise – both aspects critical to supporting Singaporean creative freelancers as breadwinners and pillars for their families.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, devices like smart kiosks have allowed eateries to operate a single site with fewer employees.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: In response to lean staffing and technology advancements, redesigned food services jobs – whether service crew, kitchen assistant or outlet manager – would likely see a shift towards an increase in the scope and responsibilities of roles.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Given the faster pace of change and wider scale of technology adoption, a refreshed social compact must include measures to help low-wage Singaporean workers, who may be less literate in English language and digital skills, deal with the stresses and expectations arising from the increased scope and responsibilities of their job roles.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: I would thus like to urge the Government and industry stakeholders to prioritise connecting low-wage workers with training that can help these vulnerable workers to pivot to the refreshed job scopes or to new career paths if their jobs will likely be replaced by automation.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: I would also like to urge employers to take a broader and longer-term view when making business plans; planning for the future must go beyond investing in automation and ought to extend into capability building and increasing accessibility to work to help these workers to balance work/life needs.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, low-wage workers could be more willing to pivot if their employer had catered adequate training and the time to build these workers' competence in interacting with emerging technologies and changing customer demands.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: These workers could also be more prepared to stay on in the job if their employers offered flexi-work arrangements that could allow these workers to manage work around their needs at different life situations.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Such moves would give cause for optimism than worry of job displacement; it would also boost the confidence of these vulnerable breadwinners in facing the challenge of technology advancement and stressful life situations head-on.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: To conclude: for many of us, around one-third of our lives would be spent working.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Work gives us dignity, income security and boosts our feelings of self-worth.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: As a whole-of-society, we must step up to the plate in our roles as Government, employers, unions and more, to give these groups of fellow Singaporeans a leg-up to start and raise their families well, and to imbue confidence in these families that they, too, can access support to thrive and find joy in their journey through life.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As we call for the continued review and updating of policies to better support families, we must confront two pressing challenges.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The first is how social media is reshaping our children's minds and relationships in ways we are only beginning to understand.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The second is more structural; the daily challenges faced by families raising children with disabilities, challenges that often remain invisible to many.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The first: protecting youth development in a digital age.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Since 2021, one key focus in our Telok Blangah Division is "Building Stronger Families".

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This commitment is reflected in a range of initiatives, including father-child programmes, a curated Mental Health Series, support for caregivers and initiatives to enhance seniors' well-being.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In 2021, we also launched the "Telok Blangah Mentoring Club", designed to journey with our youths aged 11 to 17.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: And after decades of working with them, I have grown increasingly concerned about the impact of smartphones and social media on their well-being.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The effects are real and harmful when left unchecked.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I intend to dedicate a significant part of my speech to safeguarding our young in the digital age, particularly amid the challenges of social media.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I recently addressed this topic during the Edusave 2025 as well as Bursary Award Ceremonies.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: A good number of parents and older youths later approached me to share similar concerns.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: It is clear that this issue resonates deeply with our community, highlighting the urgent need for collective action and support.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Unchecked social media use does not just change how our children communicate, it rewires how they see themselves.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As Jonathan Haidt powerfully puts it in his book "The Anxious Generation": "The rise of social media isn't merely a passing trend but a seismic shift in how young people relate to themselves and each other." Recent studies have shown that frequent social media use can significantly impact adolescent brain development, with heavy usage linked to poor mental health and increased social isolation among young people.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In contrast, youths who spend more time outdoors, engaging with others and connecting with nature tend to develop stronger mental resilience and better social skills.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This contrast underscores the need for regulators and parents to view social media with enlightened eyes; to see it not as harmless entertainment, but a force that can make or break the well-being of our young people.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: We must therefore approach it with awareness and responsibility.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In fact, we should scrutinise social media with the same vigilance as products that pose risks to our health.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Just as governments regulate tobacco to protect public health and parents limit junk food to safeguard their children's well-being, we must take decisive steps to shield our young from the mental health risks of unchecked social media use.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The stakes are too high to ignore; stronger measures are not just an option, but a necessity.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Australia equips parents with tools to manage children's screen time via the "eSafety Commissioner".

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Singapore must continue to take steps to ensure our children will not be trapped in a digital world that constantly compares them with often impossible standards.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Singapore has rolled out initiatives such as the Cyber Wellness and Digital Literacy programmes.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This recommendation, supported by the research of Mr Haidt, is not arbitrary; it is rooted in the critical stage of brain development during adolescence.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The prefrontal cortex, which plays a crucial role in regulating emotions and controlling impulsive behaviour, does not fully develop until around age 25.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I am not suggesting that social media should be off-limits until adulthood.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: But science does show that the older the teens are, the better they can manage their emotions and navigate the complexities of digital spaces.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Until then, unchecked exposure to social media can easily undermine their self-worth and emotional well-being.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Just as we delay giving teens the keys to a car or access to bear arms, we must also delay their entry into the world of social media.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The older they are, the better equipped they will be to handle the pressures that social media often amplifies, such as comparison, anxiety, insecurity and envy.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Even in the absence of legislation, I urge parents to delay social media exposure and stay vigilant about what their teens are engaging with online.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: To help teens disconnect from social media and nurture their overall well-being, we must create more opportunities for outdoor play and physical activity.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Finland offers a great example by integrating outdoor play into its school curriculum, recognising its profound benefits on mental and physical health.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Closer to home, I am inspired by Blangah Rise Primary School, where some classrooms intentionally open to a garden.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Each morning, the teachers take their students to the garden to explore nature, gifting them a peaceful outdoor space.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This simple yet powerful practice supports a holistic development.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This change allows children to explore sports without the added pressure of performance, fostering a more inclusive and enjoyable experience.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: However, many secondary school students still face barriers to participating in sports CCAs.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Parents have shared that it remains challenging for their children to join sports they are interested in or want to try, as trials are still required in some schools, even for non-competitive participation.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: At this stage of their development, when a teen expresses interest in taking up a sport, our response should be, "yes, come and try", not "sorry, you're not good enough".

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: How many parents have seen their teen come home dejected after being turned away because they were not considered "good enough"?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Could there be a deeper connection between young people turning inward to social media to channel their energy, energy that could be far better directed towards sports that not only promote physical health but also foster real-world social connections?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: How might MOE review the secondary school CCA system, to ensure that every student who wishes to engage in a sport beyond Physical Education classes has the opportunity to do so?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: At the same time, I acknowledge the practical challenges the Ministry faces, such as limited resources and logistical constraints.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Nevertheless, we can explore solutions that balance these realities while ensuring all students have access to physical activities that energises them.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: While some experienced minor inconveniences, the majority reported improved focus, better sleep, more meaningful family conversations and increased time spent outdoors with friends.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: For this initiative to succeed, the disconnection must be paired with opportunities for authentic human connections.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Without these, even the best intentions risk falling short.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Our schools and families must collaborate to make this happen.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: We need to provide easy access to opportunities like sports, community volunteering and other meaningful pursuits that encourage real-life interaction.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Parents play a crucial role in shaping a child's relationship with technology.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: One of the most effective ways to counter social media's negative effects is by encouraging outdoor activities as a regular part of family life.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: If I may be clear about this, the solution is not adding more structured activities to already packed schedules.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: A conversation with two clinical psychologists revealed something startling.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: They each had different teenagers share with them, saying: "A dog's life is better than mine; at least they have time to rest and play." Think about the weight of that statement.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: These youths were not just making casual observations.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: They see how family pets receive affection, rest and the freedom to play, while they feel they have to earn affection and rest through achievements.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The encouraging news is that many families are already making unstructured outdoor activities a regular part of the family life, whether through walks, cycling or simply spending time together at a nearby park – and Singapore is blessed with many amazing parks.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I hope parents will continue to prioritise regular family outings and protect their time with their children.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Being a teenager today is challenging and being a parent of one may be even more demanding.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In an era where screens dominate nearly every aspect of daily life, it is crucial for parents to have the right tools to set clear boundaries around screen time.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: If they notice their parents are not addicted to their devices, they may just follow suit.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Parents must be intentional in modelling healthy tech habits.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Instead, we must take back control over how we use them.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: A friend of mine practices what is referred to as "digital Sabbath", where she turns off her phone for a significant period each day to be fully present with her children.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This simple, yet powerful habit has become a precious gift for her family.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I love this same question families can ask at the dinner table daily: "what is one good thing that happened to you today?" We can expand initiatives that empower parents with strategies for creating screen-free zones at home while also helping them monitor and guide their children's online activity.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: By equipping parents with these tools, we can foster healthier relationships with technology, benefiting both teens and parents.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I have seen this shift happening in some of my residents.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: During house visits, I have observed families making conscious effort to use phones and computers only in shared spaces, like the living or dining room.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This is such a wise practice and I sure hope it becomes the norm across all families.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Just as parents know exam schedules and school entry requirements, they should also learn how to help their children navigate the digital world responsibly.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Parents also need to feel equipped to have open conversations about the risks and benefits of technology and social media, especially when it comes to mental health.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: These discussions are urgent during the pre-teen and teen years, when children are most vulnerable.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: More importantly, parents can create space where their children feel comfortable sharing their online experiences and emotions, free from judgement.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: A friend of mine only recently learned, in an open conversation with her son, that he had been severely bullied online when he was 13.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: She now understands why he struggled with anxiety attacks and depression throughout his teenage years and into junior college.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: We must not be afraid to get help.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Parents need to be equipped to recognise these challenges early.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I am always blessed when parents approach me, unafraid to seek help in this area.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: They come fully aware of how social media and constant digital communication have impacted mental health.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I will now move to the second pressing challenge: supporting families of children with disabilities.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Beyond screen time concerns, another group I am concerned about are families of children with disabilities.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: We must not forget this special group and ensure they receive support through every stage of caregiving.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I also look forward to the expansion of the Enabling Services Hubs, for which I am very, very grateful.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This will provide much-needed respite for caregivers of persons with disabilities (PwDs).

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As I have highlighted in previous speeches, FWAs are not merely a preference for caregivers.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This group, in particular, faces a unique set of challenges.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: They need steady income to support children with high and often complex support needs.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Despite being educated, competent and possessing a diverse range of skills, many caregivers find themselves in jobs that under-utilise their talents and pay them significantly less simply because these positions offer the flexibility they desperately need.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Faced with the demands of both childcare and job hunting, caregivers of children with severe disabilities are often forced to accept whatever opportunity comes their way, regardless of whether it aligns with their qualifications or financial needs.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Just as SG Enable works with companies to facilitate employment for PwDs, could they consider expanding their efforts to include caregivers of individuals with severe disabilities and rare disorders?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: These caregivers possess valuable skills and experience that, with the right accommodations, could greatly benefit both the workforce and the companies that hire them.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The challenges facing our youth and families of children with disabilities are deeply intertwined.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: We must not only protect our young people from the harmful effects of social media but also empower them to build resilience and emotional strength for the future.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: At the same time, we will stand with families who are navigating the complexities of raising children with disabilities, offering consistent and meaningful support.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: These are not issues that can be solved with temporary fixes or half-measures.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: They demand our sustained commitment, compassion and urgent action.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: My hope is that we can create a future where every person and every family can flourish in their own lane.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, I like to focus my speech today on how the Government can do even more to support parents with the financial costs of raising children.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In this way, young parents across the board, whether higher- or lower-income, can benefit from $100 less in full-day childcare fees every month.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And so, a parent at roughly the 35th income percentile, with per capita income monthly of $2,250, would pay $108 every month, instead of $208 currently at an Anchor Operator centre.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And a parent at median income, with per capita monthly income of $3,000, would pay $239 every month, instead of $339 currently.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Indeed, beyond the specifics, what I would also like to put forth is a refreshed benchmark – a new definition – of affordable childcare in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Today, affordability is defined as a dual-income family with a child in Anchor Operator full-day childcare paying around the equivalent of primary school and student care fees.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I think we can and should go further.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Today, the maximum CDA dollar matching from Government for a first child is $4,000.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But the bottom line is this: $4,000 contribution from parents into the CDA should be able to cover four full years of childcare from three to six years old, if the parents are at median income and the child is with an Anchor Operator.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This is my suggestion for a refreshed benchmark for affordable childcare in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Think of this as an extension of the CDA, which supports our children in their preschool years.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, as they enter and step through their formal schooling years, my suggestion is to extend the CDA and support them with a Child Development cash bonus in their primary and secondary school years.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Because the latest statistics tell us that educational expenses for our children do not quite drop after their preschool years, when they enter their formal schooling years.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Indeed, our families are spending, on average, roughly $600 every month on private tuition for their school-going children.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: To be clear, I am not passing judgement on whether or how much, private tuition is appropriate.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Indeed, I am just looking at the facts, looking at the actual cost burdens that our parents today are facing and suggesting a way in which we can better support our parents in the face of these realities.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And I believe that, ultimately, parents all want to do their best for their children and give the best to their children, and what is "best" can be very personal and varies from individual to individual.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, those who spend on private tuition do so, because they want the best for their children.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And the reality is tuition is a key cost driver today for raising children in Singapore and so we ought to lean in and help.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I believe that $600 every year, this cash bonus for every student, will go some way towards helping our parents and yet contain the risk of unintended inflationary effects on the private tuition market or, indeed, on any other area that our parents may choose to spend on, to provide the best for their school-going children.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: My third suggestion is on how to fund my first two suggestions – for both higher childcare subsidies and cash bonuses for school-going children.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Specifically, I like to suggest that we create a new Future Generations Package, with a new Future Generations endowment fund, to fund these two suggestions in perpetuity.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, put together, around $400 million each year and my suggestion is to set aside a new endowment to fund these in perpetuity.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We have set aside $8 billion for the Pioneer Generation Package, $6 billion for the Merdeka Generation Package and $7 billion for the Majulah Package, all to take good care of our seniors and, rightly so.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I think it is about time that we also have a package for our children today and those yet to be born – a Future Generations Package, for our future generations.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Set aside a package, to send a strong signal of this Government's commitment to our future generations and to the parents who are, or will be, nurturing these future generations.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: As with our past packages for seniors, the commitments in this Future Generations Package should be fully funded by the Government of the day, with funds set aside from its term of Government, so that future Governments are not burdened by these commitments.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Well, for families at the lowest income decile, that is, with per capita monthly income of up to $750, there is one tier of Government subsidies for childcare, and one tier of financial assistance for school-going children, namely MOE's Financial Assistance Scheme.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: If we go to the next income decile, there are another five tiers of fee assistance for student care.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And for families in this income decile with per capita monthly income of $1,125, student care can cost almost $250 per child per month, after fee assistance.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I think we can be more consistent and more client-centric across our financial assistance policies for children.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, I urge the Government to review, streamline and harmonise our framework of student care fee assistance to make it more consistent and more client-centric, and to increase and enhance the fee assistance to lower-income families to make student care more affordable.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Three, create a new Future Generations Package; set up a new Future Generations endowment fund; to send a strong signal of the Government's commitment to our children, both born and yet to be born.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And four, make student care more affordable for our low-income families and streamline and harmonise our framework of student care fee assistance for these families.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Over the years, the council renamed itself as the Families for Life Council, to better reflect its evolving approach to connect with Singaporean families.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Families for Life Movement rallies community partners and employers in promoting marriage and parenthood programmes in the community and at workplaces.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I commend the work that the MSF has put in, in helping to grow the Families for Life Movement.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: However, we must also acknowledge that more can be done, given how Singapore's TFR has continued to trend downwards, despite the various initiatives to encourage more Singaporeans to have families.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Over the years, I have provided various suggestions in this House on how we can strengthen marriages and ease the anxieties that many young couples face when making the decision on whether to start a family.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I wish to use this opportunity to reiterate my various suggestions under three buckets.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: They are: one, providing families with greater work-life balance; two, provide better support for parenthood; and three, more support for lower-income families.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: First, on the need to provide workers and their families with greater work-life balance.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: During my regular house visits and community engagements in my Radin Mas constituency, I have spoken to many young couples and grassroots volunteers about what we can do better to encourage more Singaporeans to start families, to have babies, to have more babies.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: One common theme has surfaced, which is the importance of having work-life balance, so that they can have enough quality time with their spouse and their children.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Such sentiments are also reflected in the findings by NTUC's Youth Taskforce, which found that work-life balance ranks top of the list of concerns for our youth workforce.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: A survey by the NTUC-Singapore National Employers Federation Professionals, Managers and Executives (PMEs) Taskforce similarly found that the lack of a work-life balance was one of the top three challenges at work cited by our PMEs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: According to a November 2024 policy brief from A*STAR's Institute for Human Development and Potential, preschool children who spend extended hours – and that is, over 40 hours a week – in preschools suffer in terms of their academic performance.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Not just quality time, but more quality time.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Since I first raised the issue of the "right to disconnect" in this House in 2020, I am glad that the Government has taken steps to help provide workers with avenues to improve their work-life balance.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Since 2020, more countries have adopted their own "right to disconnect" legislation.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In addition to European countries like France, Belgium and Spain, Australia, too, passed laws in 2024 to allow workers to disconnect after work.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The momentum for clear "right to disconnect" legislation is growing globally.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Employers play a key role in providing work-life balance.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I urge all employers in Singapore to implement a "right to disconnect" policy at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I hope that we can show the world that we do not need legislation for workers to have a basic "right to disconnect" from work, to be able to spend quality time with their family and, more importantly, so that our parents do not need to leave their young children for extended hours at the childcare centre and as the hon Member Miss Rachel Ong aptly put it, "let us disconnect to connect." So, how can we provide better support for parenthood?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: What can we do more to help working parents better cope with the stressors of balancing between family life and work?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The quality and accessibility of preschool education is a key form of parenthood support.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Today, many working parents send their young children to preschools, preferably one that is affordable and near to home.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The hon Member Mr Xie Yao Quan has touched quite extensively on preschool affordability.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I will cover the need to improve the quality of our preschool education and the need to ramp up supply of preschool placements in areas where many young families are moving in.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I have said this many times: being an early childhood educator is tough work.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In addition to caring and handling a class full of energetic toddlers, preschool teachers today also do lesson preparation, administrative work, classroom set-up and attend training.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: To manage cost, many preschools operate on a lean workforce.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I understand that hiring relief staff adds cost to the preschool operations and some operators may be reluctant to do so.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Previously in this House, I asked about ECDA's efforts to ensure that all our preschools are adequately resourced.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: According to a 2015 research paper that studied the impact of students per teacher on student achievement, lower teacher-to-child ratios are beneficial for children.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: ECDA had also announced, in 2021, new initiatives to establish more inclusive classrooms and equip our preschools with the necessary resources to better support children with developmental needs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I, therefore, urge MSF to review and to lower the teacher-to-child ratio, so that more teachers and more para-educators will be required at each preschool.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We can, and we must, do more to increase the supply of preschool teachers, which would directly result in higher quality preschool education.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: On this front, I would like to commend MSF for taking on the many suggestions to make early childhood educators a profession of choice.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But we do need to continue to pay close attention to the hygiene factors at the preschools that cause our teachers to leave.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We must also ramp up the supply of preschools in towns where we expect an influx of young families.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Even mature towns like Radin Mas would require a ramp up of preschools, as the Government redevelops estates, like Redhill, through the Selective En bloc Redevelopment Scheme programme.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Supply must be built well ahead of demand, so that parents do not need to worry about infant care and childcare when they move in and start their families.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: That means that one in 10 children do not attend preschool.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Does the Government have data on the profiles of households who are not sending their children for early childhood education?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Do we know the reasons behind their reluctance to send them to school?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: How can we better support the families to send their children to preschool?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I first raised concerns about this at the Committee of Supply last year and had asked if MSF could do more to support children from lower-income households to attend preschool.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Can MSF provide an update if this has helped to increase the preschool participation rate for these families?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While we acknowledge that the Government has done much over the years in supporting Singaporeans who wish to have a family, we can do more to help address some of the structural issues that discourage Singaporeans from having children.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Special care must also be taken to help our lower-income families.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This year is SG60, an important milestone year in our nation's history.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: They should be accorded with benefits under the enhanced marriage and parenthood measures that will come into effect from 1 April 2025.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Parents with children born in the first quarter of 2025 should also be entitled to the same SG60 baby bonuses that have yet to be announced.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Families are the foundation of our nation and the policies we craft today must pave the way for generations to thrive.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
