speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In workplaces, we have been working with tripartite partners and community partners such as Families for Life Council to encourage employers to foster family-friendly practices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: For instance, we work closely with CapitaLand to support its commitment to foster work-life balance and strengthen family bonding, such as offering Families for Life lunchtime talks and organising family days for its employees.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Mr Zhulkarnain has suggested launching campaigns to normalise fathers' involvement and challenge stereotypes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum also suggested having programmes that challenge and shift traditional gender norms.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: To this end, we work closely with our partners such as the Centre for Fathering, who runs an annual "Great Companies for Dads Award" which engages and recognises organisations that nurture a family-friendly work culture through policies and initiatives that support fathers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Ms Joan Pereira suggested instituting guidelines on the extension of childcare service hours to accommodate working parents.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Under ECDA’s Code of Practice, childcare centres must operate from 7.00 am to 7.00 pm on weekdays, which are typical work hours.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Many childcare educators are parents themselves and they also need to go home on time to be with their families.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Employers should play their part to support parents who have school-going children, by providing a family-friendly work environment that supports employees in managing work and caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Minister of State Gan Siow Huang will share more about support for families via employment and workplace practices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng suggested promoting activities that unite families.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Last year, the Families for Life Council expanded the annual National Family Week into a month-long National Family Festival for the first time.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The festival not only celebrates families and reinforces their importance but also brings together more than 200 partners from the public, private, and community sectors together to rally around this cause.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Besides the National Family Festival, the Families for Life Council also organises activities to encourage family bonding and promote family values throughout the year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: (In Mandarin):   A declining TFR is not unique to Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: TFR of the 38 OECD countries has decreased from 3.3 children per woman in 1960, to 1.5 in 2022.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: As a small country, TFR is even more of a survival challenge in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Human resources have always been our most important and cherished asset.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Supporting Singaporeans to build and raise family is a critical national task.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: A "Singapore Made for Families" is the Government's initiative to mobilise society-wide efforts to support families.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Creating a truly family-friendly environment in Singapore is not just the Government's responsibility.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We also need support from all sectors of society, including employers, businesses and community partners.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Through frequent communication with Singaporeans, I understand that many are pondering how to balance work and life, and how to manage the cost of raising children.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Empathising with the people, the Government must take public sentiment into consideration and strive to reduce the cost of raising children for families.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In this regard, we have enhanced the Baby Bonus Scheme to help alleviate various childcare expenses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We also provide substantial subsidies for children's education from preschool to secondary school.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Each child will receive over $200,000 in education subsidies, with even larger sums for tertiary education.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: As mentioned by the Prime Minister at last year's National Day Rally, we will introduce a new scheme for larger families.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Specific details will be announced in this year's Budget.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Some Members have suggested FWAs and support for working parents.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Government has recently introduced a new initiative addressing these issues.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We urge companies to empathise with employees and provide more FWAs for those with family care needs, helping them to achieve the dual goal of pursuing career aspirations and spending quality time with their family.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: During this term of Government, we have increased efforts to help married couples own their homes, enabling them to start new lives and build family together.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Specific measures include significantly increasing public housing supply, reducing waiting time, and enhancing housing grants and subsidies to ensure that public housing prices remain affordable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: By addressing the practical challenges that young parents may face, we hope to provide better support for them to start a family with greater peace of mind, based on their individual circumstances, needs and preferences. : The Government remains committed to supporting Singaporean families across different needs, from building strong family relationships and managing child-raising costs, to uplifting those who require additional support.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We will continue to review our policies and programmes to ensure that they remain relevant in supporting our families.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: As a mother of three children, I can relate to most of the challenges that parents feel, especially those who are working, in managing both their work and family responsibilities at the same time.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The Government is working with employers to make workplaces more conducive for employees with young children.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I agree with Mr Yip Hon Weng, Mr Desmond Choo, Ms Joan Pereira, Mr Leong Mun Wai, Miss Rachel Ong and Ms Yeo Wan Ling that FWAs support parents in managing work and family commitments.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: On one hand, we want to contribute to the best of our abilities at work and also progress in our careers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: At the same time, we want to devote time and attention to help them to grow healthily and happily.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We often think of work-from-home arrangements, or flexi-place, whenever FWAs are mentioned.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: However, flexi-time, such as staggered work hours, or flexi-load arrangements, such as part-time work, can also be very helpful.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: In the past when FWAs were not so common, working parents often had to take leave to bring the child for a medical appointment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: For FWAs to work well, trust and communication are needed from both parties.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Employers should assess requests for FWAs based on business grounds and communicate the outcome of the assessment to the employees, while employees should be open to exploring mutually acceptable solutions if employers are unable to accede to the original request for FWAs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Instead, our approach is in enabling companies to implement FWAs sustainably, such as through job redesign and equipping of HR professionals with relevant tools and knowledge to implement FWAs sustainably.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Ms Joan Pereira and Mr Zhulkarnain spoke about the critical role fathers play and call on companies to provide FWAs to working fathers as well.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Miss Rachel Ong highlighted the importance of FWAs for caregivers of children with disabilities or rare disorders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The Tripartite Guidelines allow all employees, including fathers and caregivers, to request for FWAs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I encourage working parents and other caregivers to discuss with their employers how they can use FWAs to work productively while managing their caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: For employers, FWAs are available too, to attract and retain talented employees who may otherwise choose to switch roles or sectors or leave the workforce entirely to take care of their children, MOM is working closely with our tripartite partners to build employers capabilities and confidence in implementing FWAs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I will provide further update on this at the upcoming Committee of Supply.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: While FWAs and leave provisions are useful in helping working parents balance their dual responsibilities, some parents may also choose to take a temporary break from their career to focus on raising their children.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: However, once they are ready to return to work, many former stay-at-home parents find themselves doubting if they are still employable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: They may need some help to polish up their interview skills or update their CVs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Some need a confidence boost as they navigate a job market that has evolved in the years since they were away.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: More crucially, many worry that their skills are no longer relevant in the workplace.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This is especially so, given the rapid pace of change in the workplace due to technological shifts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This can also happen to some freelancers and lower-skilled workers whose jobs are at risk of being disrupted due to artificial intelligence and new technologies, as highlighted by Ms Jean See.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I encourage those who plan to return to regular work to make use of the wealth of resources available.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Those aged 40 and above receive higher subsidies of up to 90% and are eligible for further support under the SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Women are often the ones taking career breaks for caregiving, although men are increasingly stepping up to take on a more equal share of childcare responsibilities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Desmond Choo urged companies to provide more opportunities to help stay-home mothers return to work and he mentioned several good examples.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: There are also many programmes to support women in rejoining the workforce after a career break.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: NTUC's Women Supporting Women Mentorship Programme, as well as the "C U Back at Work" Programme which Ms Yeo Wan Ling mentioned earlier, also provide support for mothers who are returning to work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: These initiatives provide a wide-ranging ecosystem of support in preparing mothers for a successful return to work, and I strongly encourage them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Beyond individual programmes, we must also continue our broader efforts to foster a workplace culture that supports parents and families.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We encourage employers to have open conversations with their employees to help them succeed at work while they navigate parenthood.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Mark Lee will be happy to hear that the IHRP organises online and physical engagement sessions to equip both HR professionals and business leaders with the relevant skills and resources needed to implement work-life harmony measures.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I encourage organisations to join IHRP as a corporate partner and have their HR teams certified to advance progressive HR practices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Separately, the Singapore National Employers Federation offers training and resources for employers on building their HR capabilities to implement FWAs .

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum suggested introducing a Corporate Family Responsibility Certification programme to recognise companies that implement family-friendly policies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Today, companies that implement progressive workplace practices may already apply for the Tripartite Standard on Work-Life Harmony and exemplary organisations are recognised under the "Work-Life Excellence" category of the Tripartite Alliance Award.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Melvin Yong urged all employers to implement a "right to disconnect" policy at the workplace.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This has been debated before and Members had recognised it is not straightforward to impose across all jobs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Instead, as recommended under the Tripartite Advisory on Mental Health and Well-Being at Workplaces, companies should provide clarity on after-hours work communication.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This includes understanding the need for proper rest outside of work and establishing clear and reasonable expectations for work-related communication after hours.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We will do our best to create a vibrant economy with a highly skilled workforce so that there will continue to be good jobs and job security for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai may wish to review the facts and data that MOM has presented on multiple occasions in this House that show how employment rates and wage growth for Singaporeans have been on a positive trend and unemployment rate for Singapore Citizens has remained low at around 3% on average, over the last decade.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We are open to all suggestions, although these solutions must go beyond short-term and must address underlying problems, such as mindsets at the workplace about commitment level of colleagues who have young children.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We should also be careful about unintended consequences such as increasing reliance on foreign manpower or negative impact on employability of working parents in the long term.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: It is more sustainable for businesses to adjust their processes and build workplaces that can better attract and retain valuable talent from our pool of working parents.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: In this regard, we look towards partnerships with trade associations and chambers and the broader business community, in raising awareness of best practices and engendering progressive practices among employers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This is also part of the social compact that we would like to see in companies under Forward SG.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Together with our tripartite partners, we have made great strides in the past decade to foster family-friendly workplaces that have helped working parents succeed in their careers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Nonetheless, there are those who worry that parenthood may itself be a reason for employers to discriminate them at work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: It does so during all stages of the employment process, including hiring, promotion, appraisals and dismissals.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This is a significant step forward in entrenching fair and harmonious norms at the workplace that give working parents the reassurance they need to focus and to do their job well.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: On education, I know that some parents feel that our education system is stressful and worry whether their children can do well, and how to support them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We want to assure Singaporeans and parents that we have a robust system in place that supports our children every step along their education journey.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Assoc Prof Razwana asked for a review of the Singapore education system.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai suggested the removal of PSLE to reduce pressure in the education system.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This has been raised by other Members in the past, including Ms Denise Phua.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The Member may want to refer to MOE's Committee of Supply debates in 2023 and 2024 to better appreciate the considerations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: There is now greater flexibility and customisation to allow our children to discover and develop their unique strengths and interests and fulfil their potential at their own pace.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Miss Rachel Ong asked for a review of our secondary school CCA system to provide more opportunities for students to engage in physical activities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We need bold moves in organisations and our policies but at the same time, we also need to be bold in rethinking our priorities, how we define success, our mindsets and also our culture.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We also want to make Singapore a place that is made for families, but we know that the Government cannot do this on our own.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Everyone can play a part in supporting parents and also all Singaporeans to give their best at work while raising children.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This has been echoed by many of the suggestions and proposals made by Members in the House today.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Supporting Singaporeans in starting and raising families has and continues to be a top national priority.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Families are the building blocks of our society.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: They are our first line of support and a key pillar of our social compact.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: At an individual level, our families are the ones who give our lives meaning and purpose.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Globally, family formation and fertility rates have run into headwinds.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: All around the world, not just in Singapore, more are delaying marriage or not marrying at all, and even if they are married, more are having children later, having fewer children or not having children at all.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Reasons include changing societal norms around marriage and parenthood, prioritisation of careers and other life goals, and concerns about the demands of child-raising.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: After all, the decision to marry and have children is a deeply personal one.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But we know from our surveys that the majority of Singaporeans aspire to get married and have children.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is encouraging and gives hope for the future.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have engaged Singaporeans to understand their thoughts about marriage and parenthood.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Many of their concerns and challenges have been debated and discussed in the Chamber today, namely, housing, costs, competitive stress and time.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Housing, because couples want a home of their own; costs, as in the costs of raising children; competitive stress, particularly in education and time, which is perhaps the most precious commodity of all, covering a multitude of issues, including caregiving and managing work alongside family commitments.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Members may access the factsheet through the MP@SGPARL App as well.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The first step for many couples is to secure their own home, where they can build a new life together and start a family.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Supporting first-time married applicants is a key priority of our public housing policies.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We set aside up to 95% of our public flat supply for first-timers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We started this term of Government in the middle of the COVID-19 pandemic, which severely disrupted our building programme and caused a public housing crunch.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, through the efforts of HDB and the Ministry of National Development (MND) working with the built environment sector, we are now back on track.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We are also launching over 5,500 Sale of Balance (SBF) flats later this month.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: SBF flats tend to have shorter waiting times, which will help families who are looking to move into a new home more quickly.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: To help reduce the waiting time for flats, we committed to launching 2,000 to 3,000 Shorter Waiting Time (SWT) flats every year.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We met the target last year with the launch of 2,800 SWT flats.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms Hazel Poa has asked if we can further increase the supply of SWT flats.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This year, we aim to exceed our target, with 3,800 such flats, and we will continue to explore launching more SWT flats in coming years.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Collectively, these moves have helped to bring down median waiting times to pre-COVID levels of three to four years, compared to four to five years during the peak of the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Several Members have asked if this could be further reduced down to even 18 months.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There are practical and operational challenges to further shortening waiting times.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These include difficult site conditions, extensive land preparation required, need for consultation with stakeholder groups and construction industry capacity.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai suggested providing a "quality rental option" for couples waiting for the new flats in the form of the Millennial Apartments Scheme.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We do have quality rental options for this group.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is called the Parenthood Provisional Housing Scheme (PPHS).

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked about relaxing the criteria and increasing the supply of flats under the PPHS to help those who need a place while waiting for their BTO flat.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As flat supply is limited, the reality is that we will still have to prioritise PPHS flats for those with greater needs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That said, we will double the number of PPHS flats to 4,000 units by this year.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In the meantime, we have introduced the PPHS (Open Market) Voucher as a temporary bridging measure to support households renting an HDB flat or bedroom on the open market.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The voucher defrays around 10% of the median 3-room flat rent, or 40% of the cost of renting a HDB bedroom.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Around 160 couples have applied for the voucher to date.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have also been working hard to improve accessibility of BTO flats.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We introduced the First-Timer (Parents and Married Couples), or FT(PMC), priority category to help young married couples and families with young children secure their first homes more quickly.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Since introduction, about nine in 10 FT(PMC) applicants have been invited to book a flat at each sales launch.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have also made significant moves to keep HDB housing affordable.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: To help younger couples who are entering the job market but have not yet started to earn and build up their savings to get flats early, we introduced the Deferred Income Assessment scheme and the Staggered Downpayment Scheme for full-time students and National Servicemen.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We also made a major move last year to introduce the new HDB flat classification framework.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The increased subsidies for Plus and Prime flats make flats in these locations more affordable for Singaporean couples.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We also enhanced housing subsidies and grants for first-time buyers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These include the Enhanced CPF Housing Grant (EHG), the CPF Housing Grant for Resale Flats and the Proximity Housing Grant.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We know there are still concerns about the resale market.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms Hany Soh raised concerns about the Cash Over Valuation (COV) component.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Resale housing prices have risen over the last few years, driven by strong demand as well as some temporary tightness in the supply of new MOP-ed flats.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These flats also tended to be in more attractive or central locations last year.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Nevertheless, the vast majority of resale flats remain affordable and most resale flat buyers do not have to pay any COV.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have also implemented several rounds of cooling measures to moderate demand, while increasing support for lower- to middle-income households.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These measures will take time to work their way through the market.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng suggested indexing our grants to the resale market.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We do not do so as this could inadvertently further fuel resale price increases.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, some sellers may attempt to factor in grant increases in their asking price.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is why we are careful in reviewing grant amounts in tandem with income growth and affordability outcomes and means-test our grants to target support towards buyers who need it the most.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As he spoke in Malay, please permit me to reply in Malay. :   Mr Faisal asked us to allow parents who are undergoing divorce and in urgent need of housing to apply for public rental housing before the divorce is finalised.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have made this known in a reply to a previous Parliamentary Question in November 2020.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: [Please refer to "Temporary Housing for Individuals Undergoing Divorce Proceedings Or Division of Matrimonial Assets", Official Report, 4 November 2020, Vol 95, Issue 13, Written Answers to Questions for Oral Answer not Answered by End of Question Time section.] In addition, they can also apply to buy a flat upon obtaining the interim judgment and resolving matters relating to the matrimonial property and custody of their children.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Divorcees who are buying a new flat with their children can also qualify for schemes such as the Assistance Scheme for Second-Timers (ASSIST) and the PPHS.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And beyond housing, we will also continue to support divorced parents and their children through the broad-based support measures under our Marriage and Parenthood Package, so that they can continue to thrive as with all other families.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Government will do our best to help you.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Faisal also referred to the Long-Term Visit Passes for foreign spouses and shared some concerns, such as whether the current approach of online submissions and assessments are sufficient.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will refer his feedback to the Immigration and Checkpoints Authority. : Mr Speaker, Sir, to summarise, since the start of this term of Government, despite the major disruptions brought on by COVID-19, we have kept up a strong supply and delivered new flats to home buyers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have continued to provide affordable housing; about eight in 10 first-timer families can service their monthly HDB loan instalments with CPF with little or no cash outlay.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This remained true in 2024, despite rising housing prices.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And amidst the challenges, our longstanding commitment to supporting the housing needs and aspirations of Singaporean families remains firm.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will continue to study the ideas and improve our system to support young couples as they embark on their marriage and parenthood journey.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For couples deciding whether to have children, the next big consideration is costs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is fully understandable as the costs of child-raising can add up with each subsequent child.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Several Members have called for more financial support for couples.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Today, the Government provides a wide range of financial support for families through cash payouts, grants, subsidies and other forms of support.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms Hany Soh asked if the Government could support expenses incurred before the child is born, such as prenatal check-ups.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai asked if we can allow maternity and child-bearing medical fees to be fully claimable from MediSave without limits.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Actually, it was announced in October last year, under the MediSave Maternity Package, that expectant mothers will benefit from an increase in MediSave inpatient and day surgery withdrawal limits from 1 April this year.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We set a limit because MediSave is intended to help Singaporeans offset healthcare expenses over their lifetime, especially during significant health episodes, which tend to happen during old age.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: MediSave withdrawal limits are therefore set to strike a careful balance between improving the affordability of current treatment and ensuring Singaporeans have sufficient savings for their future healthcare needs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Upon birth, each Singaporean baby receives a MediSave Grant for Newborns (MGN), which can be used to cover their MediShield Life premiums, hospitalisation and outpatient treatments.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Nationally recommended childhood vaccinations and developmental screenings at polyclinics and general practitioner clinics under the Community Health Assist Scheme (CHAS) are also fully subsidised.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In the child's early years, Government support continues in the form of the Baby Bonus Scheme, comprising the Baby Bonus Cash Gift and CDA.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These help parents to defray various child-related costs, from daily expenses to preschool and healthcare.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Taking the Baby Bonus scheme and the increased MGN together, parents can receive up to $25,000 for their first child and up to $38,000 for subsequent children.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Baby Bonus Cash Gift is paid out every year until the child turns six-and-a-half, providing sustained support over the child's early years.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Government also provides strong support for infant care and childcare as outlined by Minister of State Sun earlier.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh and Mr Leong Mun Wai suggested providing subsidies for grandparents who care for young children.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We are mindful that doing so might make such family support overly transactional and monetise family relationships.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It would be more meaningful for appreciation for grandparents to come from their children instead.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But meanwhile, we do signal our support for the care provided by grandparents through the Grandparent Caregiver Relief for working mothers whose parents or grandparents care for their children aged 12 or below.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Government support continues as our children progress through school.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Education in our national school system and Institutes of Higher Learning is highly subsidised.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: When you add in the subsidies for higher education – ITE, polytechnics and the publicly funded universities – the amount is even higher.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Students from lower- to middle-income families may access various financial assistance schemes offered by the Government, schools and institutions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For those with more children, we know that expenses for larger families can add up.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As mentioned by the Prime Minister at the National Day Rally last year, we will be introducing a new scheme for large families.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We are also doing more to foster our children's health, well-being and development.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms Hany Soh suggested providing expecting mothers with support for each stage of their pregnancy.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Last year, we launched the Child and Maternal Health and Well-being Action Plan for mothers and children, including initiatives such as mental health screening, and antenatal and postnatal support.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Over the last two years, we launched Family Nexus centres in four neighbourhoods to bring health and social services closer to families in a single location within their communities.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Services include child developmental assessments, postnatal support, and marriage and parenting workshops.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have served over 12,000 children and their parents at these sites.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The next thing that parents really need is time.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Many parents tell us they value both family and careers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: At work, they want to do their best to fulfill their responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Yet, they also need to care for their children and increasingly, their parents and grandparents too.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: When it comes to child-raising, fathers need to be involved as well.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As Ms Joan Pereira and Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim highlighted, research shows that children benefit from fathers' involvement in their early years and have positive developmental outcomes well beyond the early years.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Over the last few years, we have strengthened our support in three areas to give parents more of that precious commodity – time.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These include parental leave; infant care, childcare and student-care facilities which free up parents' time and allow them to focus on work; and FWAs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In this term of Government, we have significantly ramped up leave for parents.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We doubled Government-Paid Paternity Leave from two to four weeks.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: At the same time, we understand Mr Mark Lee and Ms Yeo Wan Ling's concern that employers, especially SMEs, may incur additional costs when making covering arrangements for employees on parental leave.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: To support employers, most of our parental leave provisions are Government-paid.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Employers can use the wage savings as they deem fit, including to offset any costs during the transition period between returning employees and covering staff.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We encourage parents to discuss their leave plans with their employers as early as possible and work with them on suitable covering arrangements.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have complemented annual leave provisions with childcare leave to cater for ad hoc situations where time off is needed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We provide more childcare leave to those with younger children, as older children are generally more independent.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Some Members have called for more childcare leave, especially for those with more children, primary school-aged children, or children with disabilities.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We can understand why families would like additional childcare leave.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: At the same time, enhancements to our leave schemes require us to strike a fine balance between the caregiving needs of these parents and other caregivers, as well as the needs of employers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Employers also need time to adjust to the new Shared Parental Leave scheme starting soon, which is more complex to administer.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, Members can be assured that we will continue to regularly review our leave policies in consultation with parents and the tripartite partners.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Tripartite Guidelines on Flexible Work Arrangement Requests which Minister of State Gan has spoken about will benefit all parents with caregiving responsibilities in a sustainable way.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: At the same time, I urge employers to ensure their workplaces are FWA friendly.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Employers should not think of FWAs as an inconvenient imposition but rather embrace it as an integral part of their HR toolkit to attract and retain talent and redesign the way your company works for greater success.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Chua suggested that we over-emphasised work over family but, on the other hand, Mr Leong Mun Wai and Ms Hazel Poa have reiterated the importance of job security to Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is why we need to strike a balance and ensure that our policies consider the needs of all stakeholders.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, the Government naturally adopts the position in between, balancing both sides.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And if you think about it, what is happening in the US now, the call to everybody to come back in the office and not to be able to work from home is really a response and a reaction to the last few years where there has been much more of working from home and we do not want that kind of backlash here.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, that is why we move, calibrating things carefully, recognising that employers' needs are important, jobs are important, incomes are important but also recognising that parents need time to be with their children.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, that is why we take this calibrated approach.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms Nadia Samdin and Ms Hazel Poa spoke about fertility and that is an important topic which the topic of parenthood cannot be divorced from the subject of fertility.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With people marrying later or delaying having children, we do need to focus much more on fertility health.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I agree with Ms Nadia that the first step is to raise awareness or factors affecting fertility health.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Second, we need to normalise discussions about fertility health.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For those who want to have children but have not been successful, the topic of infertility is often shrouded in stigma and shame and for some, a sense of personal failure.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We need to have a broader understanding that infertility can affect anyone, male or female, and should be approached in a similar manner to other health issues.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Government has stepped up fertility support in this term.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Today, women can tap on MediSave for egg freezing done on medical grounds.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We are studying if other financing support should also be extended to egg freezing done on medical grounds.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For those who wish to use their frozen eggs for assisted conception procedures in future, they can receive Government co-funding support and use MediSave for their treatments.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I wish to clarify with Mr Desmond Choo that since January 2020, women aged 40 and above can receive co-funding for up to two of the six co-funded ART cycles, as long as they have attempted an ART or intrauterine insemination procedure before age 40.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have also bolstered mental and emotional support for those undergoing fertility treatment.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Assisted Reproduction centres are required to inform patients of available counselling services prior to any assisted conception procedure and refer them for psychosocial counselling if needed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Non-government groups also have an important role to play.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Fertility Support SG is a non-profit organisation started in 2020 by a group of ladies facing infertility.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They decided to create a community of support for others with fertility issues.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They provide information, create a safe space for discussions and share experiences.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But singles are also an important group to look out for.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh and Ms Hany Soh asked if the Government could run a networking agency or app for singles to meet potential partners.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I should say that decisions around dating and romantic relationships are deeply personal.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These are certainly not things that the Government can mandate.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: What we can do, perhaps, is our best to facilitate.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Introducing a platform or app with an explicit Government signature may not be the most effective approach.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Many youths tell us they prefer to meet and interact with people in natural settings.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Today, we have a vibrant social interaction space with a wide variety of options for singles to meet new people, be it through well-established online apps, or more informal interest groups.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We welcome ground-up initiatives by partners who are keen to encourage and strengthen friendships among young people and we will provide our support where appropriate.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If we are to succeed in having more marriages and babies, we will need a whole of society approach – employers, businesses, community partners and individuals – all have a part to play too, to create a society where family is valued and parenthood is supported.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Ng has made repeated calls in this House for more lactation rooms for nursing mothers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: At his invitation, I met with the Breastfeeding Mothers Support Group to understand the challenges faced by breastfeeding mothers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They shared stories of how nursing mothers had to express in a dusty storeroom or spaces with little privacy.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And recently, a former colleague sent me a picture of what passes for a lactation room in a dispute resolution facility – basically a room with a table and chairs suitable for meetings but not really configured for a nursing mother's needs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We must consider the message that is inadvertently being sent, which is that breastfeeding, which is an integral part of motherhood, is an inconvenience and the provision of facilities for it is more of an afterthought.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That is the message that is being sent.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, I am sure there was no ill-intent on the part of building owners and employers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But the message to nursing mothers is discouraging nonetheless and at odds with a society that wants to be supportive of families.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I will share more at MND's Committee of Supply.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But the broader point is that as a society, we must think more deeply and carefully about how we can be supportive of families in ways big and small, be it from re-imagining how to structure work and adopt good HR policies to help employees manage career and parenthood, to having child-friendly infrastructure and activities for families.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In this, Families For Life and the Made For Families, which Minister of State Sun spoke about, play important roles.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Families For Life provides information, programmes and community support on marriage, parenting and grandparenting, which can also be accessed online.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I encourage families to avail themselves of these resources.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Made For Families rallies organisations to adopt family-friendly practices.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, that is still a very small number compared to the number of businesses in operation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And also work-life support: 30 weeks of paid parental leave during the child's first year after birth; and various caregiving options and FWAs for ongoing caregiving needs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For preschools, we have ramped up infant care capacity; and for education, we have also undertaken major reforms.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That is just for the early childhood sector and the upcoming parental leave enhancements.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: [Please refer to "Clarification by Minister, Prime Minister's Office, and Second Minister for Finance and National Development", Official Report, 5 February 2025, Vol 95, Issue 151, Correction By Written Statement section.] This is over and above our subsidies for general and higher education as well as our housing subsidies.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, Sir, we will continue to review and update our policies as called for by the original Motion and I want to thank Members for their ideas and suggestions, which we will certainly take into account in reviewing and updating the various policies.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The original Motion is, "That this House calls for the continued review and updating of policies to better support families, as well as the marriage and parenthood aspirations for Singaporeans and endorses a whole-of-society approach to build a Singapore Made for Families." Mr Leong's proposed amendment is to delete the words, "continued review and updating" and substitute, instead, the word "re-imagination".

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, if you do that and if you insert his amendment, it will read as follows, "That this House calls for the re-imagination of policies to better support families, as well as the marriage and parenthood aspirations for Singaporeans and endorses a whole of society approach to build a Singapore Made for Families." Ordinarily, Mr Speaker, I would have no issue with such a proposed amendment, because after all, why would one object to the idea of re-imagining something and making sure that you come up with something new; except that, in this context, there are two reasons why I would not support the amendment.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The first is that, in this context, it is actually not a step forward, it is a step back.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And second, it is tied to a policy which is problematic and let me explain why.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Why do I say that the amendment is actually a step back?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Well, it is because, in this debate, I think, Mr Leong Mun Wai, Ms Hazel Poa and Mr Louis Chua have sought to portray the marriage and parenthood measures that we have at the moment as incremental.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, in other words, not bold enough, not doing enough, therefore, you need to re-imagine something.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But the point is this: in the last few years, we have already started the re-imagination process.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is called Forward SG and if you look at what we did with Forward SG, you will see that when Forward SG was launched, then-Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said at the launch of the Forward Singapore Exercise in June 2022, that the 4G Team was going to embark on an exercise to review and refresh our social compact and chart a roadmap for the next decade and beyond.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And just before he became Prime Minister, he said in an interview with local media, we are prepared to relook everything.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is not so much that we are going to slay a sacred cow for doing so, but we are prepared to re-examine all our assumptions and consider, under different circumstances, different societal expectations and needs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And we have already started this process because the Forward SG work has already started.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, what are some of the major moves that we have done?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If you think about it, the HDB new Classification Framework.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For decades, we have had the mature and non-mature classification, but this came out of Forward SG.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We launched it last year and it is a major move that is just starting to take place and we are rolling it out, so it is actually being implemented.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The other major moves would be for preschool.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And we have also lowered the "out-of-pocket" expenses and we have had subsidy enhancements and fee cap reductions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And education – we have made big, bold changes in education under the equip pillar of Forward SG.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have now a full implementation of full subject-based banding and we are broadening the post-secondary pathways.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And in addition, we have got Shared Parental Leave.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: All these are major moves with a vision of a "Singapore Made for Families".

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, we have already started the re-imagination process.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The boat called re-imagination has already left port and is sailing.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is picking up speed and we are implementing, adding on and enhancing as we go.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, to ask us in this amendment to start re-imagination, it is kind of like a step back.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is kind of like going to the port, whereas the ship has already sailed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That is the reason why I would not agree to the amendment.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But there is a second reason and it is a bit problematic.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That is because in his speech on calling for re-imagination, Mr Leong Mun Wai has also said that we need to adopt certain policies and one of the central ones is the Affordable Homes Scheme.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I mean, the other ideas and suggestions, certainly, we can think about and explore, but the Affordable Homes Scheme is the one that removes the price of land when pricing flats upfront.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But, Sir, other than that, I really do thank Members for their support for families, their ideas and suggestions, which we will continue to take on board and I support the original Motion.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Faisal Manap, do you have a clarification?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I would just like to seek one clarification from the Minister.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: Earlier, the Minister mentioned that there are cases where HDB approved application for rental flat under the public rental scheme by individuals who are still in the midst of divorce proceedings.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: So, may I know, is there a specific scheme for this or is it across the board or just based on a case-by-case basis?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, if the Member's residents are concerned, the Member can give them the assurance that HDB will still look at their applications.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: But based on my personal dealing with the MPS cases, there are many letters, replies from HDB, which mentioned that residents have to go through the proceedings to be able to prove, to submit a divorce certificate.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: So, basically, my proposal is for HDB to actually implement a scheme for such cases.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But if there are any specific cases, then, perhaps, Mr Faisal Manap can send them to me and I will see what can be done.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I heard the Minister's reply and reference to the Parliamentary reply in 2020.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, I am just following up on what my colleague, Mr Faisal Manap, has said with regard to representations from HDB.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Just as an example: 1 May 2024, a letter written by HDB, "Your request to rent a public rental flat from HDB", and then HDB lists out the circumstances that are necessary before the rental application can be assessed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, this is what the letter from HDB says: "We have learnt that you are still legally married.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Please note that a married couple is considered as a single legal entity and we are not able to allow one party to exclude the other during the application.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In addition, HDB would not be able to consider an applicant's application if they have not obtained the deed of separation, or when the divorce is not finalised, as we would need to know the distribution of matrimonial assets, if any.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Furthermore, for divorce applicants who wish to apply for a flat with their children below 21 years old, they would need to have custody with care and control, as stated in the order of Court.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We are prepared to consider your request after you have obtained the deed of separation or the finalised divorce documents, as we need to know more on the distribution of matrimonial assets, if any, and the custody of the children." So, it would appear not to be consistent with what the Minister is sharing.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, I just thought I would put that out.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: One is that it is case-by-case, not a specific scheme.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Second, in the letter that Mr Pritam Singh referred to, it also did refer to a deed of separation, right?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, just to check, there is a difference between an application to buy a new flat and application for rental flat.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Can I just check for Mr Pritam Singh, was he talking about application to buy or application for rental?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, it would suggest that the reply from HDB ought to have said what the Minister has been sharing, because it is clearly a rental application not an application to buy.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Yes, and I believe that in the reply, Mr Singh did refer to HDB talking about a "deed of separation".

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And a deed of separation is something you can do, even before the interim judgment.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, I would like to ask the Minister, first of all, whether when we are debating the need for more policies, are we treating this as a national emergency or not?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Or is it just a business as usual, maybe we need more?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But I think the most important thing that we need to agree is that this is a very urgent problem and I would classify it as a national emergency.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, I would prefer that if you have clarifications, and you did mention that you have many clarifications, if you have clarifications, kindly raise all of them now.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Yes, yes, because the Minister has said a list of things.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, list all your clarifications so the Minister will respond to your clarifications.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Okay, first of all, I want to ascertain whether we are debating this as a national emergency or not.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The next thing is, the Minister mentioned about re-imagining.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, we raised the issue, and my colleagues from Workers' Party also agree to that, that the current policies are obviously inadequate.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: As a result, we need to have new policies and there is a basis for us to say why the current policies need re-imagining.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, I would like to ask the Minister whether she agrees that when we imagine what I have suggested in my speech, for example, we are actually trying to engage all the stakeholders, a whole-of-society approach.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The whole-of-society approach, when hearing from the office bearers, seems to be a shirking of responsibility, saying that, it is not just the responsibility of the Government, the society also has to help.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But to us, the whole-of-society approach is that you must provide more fiscal incentives, to involve more stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Does the Minister agree, that in our recommendation of the new policies, we actually consider stakeholders like the employers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: You ask the employers to have more FWAs, you ought to give them more fiscal incentives.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We talk about engaging the community, engaging the extended family, the grandparents who are giving care to the children, they ought to be renumerated.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We are trying to expand the scope of thinking.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: It is not just what the Government has been doing, just from Government to the parents.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Furthermore, we are also expanding into thinking about the mental health of the children, because happy children mean happy life.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: You should not be making any more speeches, as with any other Members.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I am not quite sure what your clarification is, but please state —

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Yes, but does she agree that our re-imagining is actually different, from the kind of re-imagining —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Okay, you can go to your next clarification.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, when we say re-imagining, we are, of course, confident that there are many gaps in the current policies of the Government.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: First of all, under helping married couples with their first home.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And that is one problem with saying the Government policies' implementation is that you always put it ahead.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: In fact, I think the policy should be to backdate one year, so as to make the parents feel that, "Hey, I had better get into the boat as soon as possible." Rather than, "Oh, I will give you the benefit in a few months' time." So, that means you cause the parents to say, "Maybe I should delay a few months and see whether maybe after Budget?"

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, can you get to your clarifications?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: You are making a lot of mini speeches here.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I have said this many times to everyone.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I allow you to make clarifications, as many as you want, but please make them and make it succinct.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: You do not have to state all your —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Your preambles are super long, are super long.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Many other members have stated their clarification in previous —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I allow Members to seek clarifications, as many as you want, but do not make mini speeches.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: You are not allowed, as with any other Member who has spoken, you are not allowed to make any more speeches.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So please, you stated you have many clarifications.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I am giving you the floor to ask all your clarifications.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, the fourth clarification is, do you think these policies ought to be implemented backdated rather than forward dated?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The fifth clarification I seek to get is, under supporting child's development and well-being, she mentioned the shift in the education system and all that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But does the Minister think that this is really sufficient?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Because I think we still got a lot of feedback from the ground that the PSLE system is still a big burden on the families.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, does she think that our suggestion of having a dual track system can achieve three objectives at the same time: one is better family life; two is better child development; and three, actually allows our children to have more social interaction time.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And the sixth point I want to make is that, in terms of helping parents to balance work and all that, does she agree that our suggestion of an enhanced job-sharing scheme has the following benefits and actually it engages the employers better rather than the current job-sharing scheme of just providing $35,000?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And the benefits of a job-sharing scheme – enhanced job-sharing scheme – does she agree that: one, it improves work life balance; two, Singapore workers can continue to be on the job without leaving the job market and that is very important.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Today, once a Singaporean leaves the job market, it is very difficult for him or her to come back, and we all know that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And three, actually, it can increase employment because it may allow a few more Singaporeans to have part of a job.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: My last question, the seventh question is, does she agree that since we want to build Singapore as a "Singapore Made for Families" and we want to involve a whole-of-society effort, the best is actually to engage the extended family and give incentives to the family and that will make our overall plan far more effective.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, that is the seventh question, does she agree that this will be a more effective way of doing it?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, in conclusion, I think what I am trying to drive at is our re-imagining is not just giving some money from Government to parents.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: It is actually involving a lot of stakeholders and incentivising them to take action towards the same objective.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First, he asked, is it a national emergency?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think it is a very important national issue. "Emergency" sort of suggests the idea of all alarm bells ringing, everybody rushing around and so on.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But our approach is when you have a serious national issue, you look at it calmly, coolly, you understand what the issues are and you then take the necessary steps to address them.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And that leads on to his next point about re-imagining, because Mr Leong said that have we engaged the stakeholders?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That is exactly what I was explaining just now.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That was the whole purpose of the Forward SG exercise and, in fact, before that, we had the Singapore Together conversations.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, the point I am making about the re-imagination process – leave aside the policies that he has suggested – the amendments made it appear as though we have not even embarked on thinking about re-imagining Singapore and my reply to that was, we have already started the re-imagination process and we have done that under Forward SG and we have done engagements.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And that would include the families, family members, parents and so on.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Then, I think the next point that Mr Leong raised was talking about whether the policies were resulting in a low TFR.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think the point I made in my speech, which I must reiterate here, is that declining TFR is a global trend.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, for example, between 2013 and 2023, I mean, when you look at all of the countries, Malaysia, France, Denmark, Sweden, UK, Japan, Singapore, South Korea, they are all on a downward trend.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Perhaps the only one that bucks the trend may be Israel, which was mentioned in one of the speeches.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Well, it has been dropping and then just had a slight tilt up.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, the point to be made is that it is not just us, which means that there is something happening at a global level and those are the reasons which I mentioned earlier.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Leong set out a list of his policies and asked whether I could agree with each one of them.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But we started this whole process, this re-imagination process before.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We talked to people to understand what their concerns were.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And their concerns were, as I mentioned in my speech: space or housing, costs for child raising, education or competitive stress and time.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, as far as the list that Mr Leong has put out of his proposed policies, those, if he is putting them forward as things which may be helpful, remember, as I mentioned in my closing of the speech, I said we can consider all of those.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I really felt that I could not support the amendment insofar as it was tied to that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But I will give her two new questions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Does that difference mean that it is a responsibility that the Government has to take?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The second question is actually the debate on the Affordable Homes Scheme is not complete.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But I do not want to extend today's debate into the Affordable Homes Scheme.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I have stated many times that I disagree that it is raid on the Reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And when the Minister says that the Affordable Homes Scheme is actually a prepaid rental scheme, is the current system not the same thing, with the 99-year lease?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Is the 99-year lease not a prepaid rental scheme as well, for 99 years?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, please, do not use Affordable Homes Scheme to negate all the debate I am trying to put up today.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: France is also on a global decline as far as TFR is concerned.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, I am not quite sure, but the suggestion seems to be that Government is responsible for 0.97 TFR.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think that that is not the case.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There are many factors which are affecting TFR and I have listed them.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Government can do its very best to facilitate and try to make sure that we have an ecosystem and an environment that is as supportive of parents and couples, and of marriage and parenthood as possible, which is exactly what we are trying to do.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Then, on the second point of Affordable Homes Scheme, I think we must certainly agree to disagree, because Mr Leong may have his view on Affordable Homes Scheme but I have mine.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And I have to explain to the Chamber why I disagree with his proposed amendment.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And his amendment, one of the key things, is the Affordable Homes Scheme and that is the part I disagree with.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Remember, I said that the other things we can discuss.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, this was the one that caused me a difficulty and that is why I am sharing it to everybody why I think that I cannot support the amendment.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But on the first question that I have asked just now, what I mean is that any phenomena that we observe, there is always a systemic factor and there is a specific factor.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Other countries have also experienced a general decline in the TFR.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But if other countries are still maintaining at 1.5 and our TFR has gone right below 1.0, that is the difference.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: You are 0.5 below some countries that we can benchmark against.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, of course, you can choose South Korea.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But South Korea is like ourselves – the whole social economy model, there are issues to it.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: That is why we are saying that there is one systemic factor here and there is a specific factor.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, I am of the view that our policies have not addressed the specific factors.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The Government is making an effort and a commitment that we must reach there.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: You cannot just say that, "Oh, everything is dropping, we can't help it".

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: More or less, you are saying that we cannot help it.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: That cannot be the case, because then, we will be really running towards an extinction.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But Mr Leong says the Government says, "Can't help it".

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, it is very odd because Mr Leong says the Government says something when the Government has not said any such thing.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, insofar as he says, set a target.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: You cannot just set a target for women to have children just like that.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I do not think that families or mothers will just produce babies just because you set them a target.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Having children is a personal decision and it is really up to parents to decide if they want to have children.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: What we can and are doing is trying to make it as facilitative and as comfortable as possible for them to do so.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I am sharing this survey because it is published data.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: It is from a survey of young persons and it is just to reinforce the point that Minister Indranee made, which is that when it comes to matters as personal as getting married and having children, it is not just like we snap our fingers and we say, "We want TFR to be this", that we can somehow command young people to go forth, get married and have children.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We have to recognise that they have their own aspirations.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I think the survey results that we have shown here is not unique to Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: All across the world, when you look at published data, when you look at interviews with young people, the aspirations of young people have changed.

speaker: Mr Speaker
